knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex minimization without explicit feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Unconstrained convex minimization is the problem
\[
p^\star:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} f(x).
\]
Its solution set is \(X^\star:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:f(x)=p^\star\}\), which may be empty unless attainment is assumed. At any query point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), a subgradient method may use \(g\in\partial f(x)\), characterized by \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function over Euclidean space, using subgradients at finite-valued query points; existence of a minimizer is an additional assumption.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Fundamentals of the Theory and Methods of Unconstrained Minimization p. 2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fermat Rule for Unconstrained Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global optimality test for the unconstrained convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. For every \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^d}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\partial f(x^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued point globally minimizes a convex function exactly when its convex subdifferential contains zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Fermat Rule for Unconstrained Convex Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Objectives Need Not Attain Their Infimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp attainment boundary for the seed problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=e^x\) is finite, continuous, proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R\), but \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=0,\qquad e^x>0\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.\] Hence \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential function is closed and convex but approaches its infimum only at infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Objectives Need Not Attain Their Infimum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Convex Minimization and Optimal Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines unconstrained minimization for a finite-valued convex function on Euclidean space. It does not assert existence or uniqueness of an optimal solution, differentiability, or nonsmoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. The unconstrained convex minimization problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\). A point \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is an optimal solution if and only if \(f(x^*)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a convex real-valued function on Euclidean space, the unconstrained problem minimizes the function over the whole space. A point is an optimal solution exactly when its value equals the infimum over that space; the definition does not guarantee that such a point exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal solution}\Longleftrightarrow x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and }f(x^*)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)

knowledge_statements.title: Simple-Set Constrained Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex minimization over a closed convex set admitting direct projection or prox operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\). Simple-set constrained minimization is
\[
p^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x),
\]
where the information model supplies an exact or prescribed-accuracy projection or prox operation over \(C\). Equivalently, it minimizes \(f+\iota_C\) over \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(\iota_C(x)=0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a proper convex objective over a nonempty closed convex set whose projection or prox operation is directly available.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
f\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple-set convex minimization with an exact first-order oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies both the feasible-set access model and the objective oracle used by projected nonsmooth first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simple-set convex minimization problem is \[\min_{x\in Q}f(x),\] where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex, \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and the Euclidean projection \[\pi_Q(z)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\|x-z\|\] is efficiently computable for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). A first-order oracle returns, at every query \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), a pair \((f(\bar x),g(\bar x))\) satisfying \(g(\bar x)\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes a convex function over a nonempty closed convex set with efficiently computable Euclidean projections. An exact first-order oracle returns the function value and a valid subgradient at every query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Oracle}(\bar x)=(f(\bar x),g(\bar x)),\qquad g(\bar x)\in\partial f(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.title: Functionally Constrained Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex minimization with feasibility represented by convex inequality functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Functionally constrained minimization is
\[
p^\star:=\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ g_i(x)\le 0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Its feasible set is \(F:=\{x\in C:g_i(x)\le 0\text{ for every }i\}\), and feasibility means \(F\ne\varnothing\). The functional-constraint information model permits queries of \(g_i(x)\) and a relative subgradient \(s_i\in\partial_C g_i(x)\), where
\[
\partial_C g_i(x):=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^d:g_i(y)\ge g_i(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a convex objective over a nonempty convex feasible set described by convex inequalities whose values and relative subgradients on the base set can be queried.

notation.meaning: subdifferential of g_i relative to C at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smallest-Root Characterization of a Constrained Optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-value characterization through the max-residual value function for one functional inequality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\ne\varnothing\), let \(f,\bar f:Q\to\mathbb R\), and assume that
\[
\min_{x\in Q}\{f(x)\mid \bar f(x)\le0\}
\]
has an optimal solution \(x^*\), with \(t^*=f(x^*)\). Define
\[
f^*(t)=\min_{x\in Q}\max\{f(x)-t,\bar f(x)\},\qquad t\in\mathbb R,
\]
and assume that \(f^*\) is nonincreasing on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(t^*\) is the smallest root of \(f^*\):
\[
f^*(t^*)=0,\qquad f^*(t)>0\quad\text{for every }t<t^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the functionally constrained problem attains the value t*, the max-residual value function equals zero at t* and is strictly positive at every smaller threshold, under the stated monotonicity assumption.

children.title: Lagrangian Dual Minimization
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth convex dual objectives generated by primal subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Dual Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex minimization form of the Lagrangian dual generated by inequality-constrained primal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. For the primal problem \(\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), define
\[
L(x,\lambda):=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x),\qquad q(\lambda):=\inf_{x\in C}L(x,\lambda).
\]
Since \(q\) is concave, its dual maximization is equivalently the convex minimization problem
\[
\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m}\phi(\lambda),\qquad \phi(\lambda):=-q(\lambda).
\]
At any \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) for which \(q(\lambda)>-\infty\) and an exact minimizer \(x_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}L(x,\lambda)\) exists, define \(g(x_\lambda):=(g_1(x_\lambda),\ldots,g_m(x_\lambda))\). Then \(-g(x_\lambda)\in\partial\phi(\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating the concave Lagrangian dual function produces a convex minimization problem, and an exact solution of a finite-valued Lagrangian subproblem supplies a subgradient equal to the negative vector of constraint values.

notation.meaning: vector of constraint values at the Lagrangian minimizer

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value relations for the convex dual minimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ g_i(x)\le0\}\), \(q(\lambda):=\inf_{x\in C}L(x,\lambda)\), and \(d^*:=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=-\inf_{\lambda\ge0}\phi(\lambda)\). Weak duality gives \(d^*\le p^*\). If \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) and there exists \(\hat x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) with \(g_i(\hat x)<0\) for every \(i\), then \(d^*=p^*\) and the dual supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual values are lower bounds on the primal value, while finite-dimensional relative Slater regularity gives zero gap and an optimal multiplier.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is nonempty and convex}
\text{For strong duality: }\exists\hat x\in\operatorname{ri}C:\ g_i(\hat x)<0\ \forall i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^*\le p^*,\qquad\text{and under relative Slater }d^*=p^*\text{ with dual attainment}
knowledge_statements.title: Weak and Slater-Strong Lagrangian Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Lagrangian Solve Gives a Relative Epsilon-Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle degradation caused by an additively inexact primal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) with finite \(q(\lambda)\). If \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) satisfies \[L(x_\varepsilon,\lambda)\le q(\lambda)+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\ge0,\] then for every \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^m\), \[\phi(\mu)\ge\phi(\lambda)+\langle-g(x_\varepsilon),\mu-\lambda\rangle-\varepsilon.\] Thus \(-g(x_\varepsilon)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient of \(\phi\) relative to \(\mathbb R_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive epsilon solution of the primal Lagrangian subproblem returns a relative epsilon-subgradient of the negative dual objective.

notation.meaning: Epsilon-subdifferential relative to the nonnegative orthant.

children.title: Value–Subgradient Oracle
children.top_down_role: The standard joint information interface supporting value-based output selection and target-level policies.

knowledge_statements.title: Value–Subgradient Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact joint objective-value and convex-subgradient information at each admissible query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and query domain \(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), an exact value–subgradient oracle maps each \(x\in Q\) to a pair \((f(x),g_x)\) with \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\). Thus its response satisfies
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The returned scalar is the exact objective value, so algorithms may compare queried points by value or use target-level rules involving \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every query point, the oracle returns the exact objective value and an exact convex subgradient satisfying the global supporting-hyperplane inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle definition is standard, precise, and appropriate for the leaf, but no cited evidence or inspectable locator supports the interface and its stated algorithmic uses.

children.title: Subgradient-Only Oracle
children.top_down_role: First-order directional information without dependable objective values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information limitation caused by the absence of objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper and convex and let \(c\in\mathbb R\). Since \[\partial(f+c)(x)=\partial f(x)\] at every query point, a subgradient-only oracle can return the same transcript for \(f\) and \(f+c\). Thus it cannot identify absolute objective values, distinguish fixed-target statements \(f(x)\le\tau\) from \((f+c)(x)\le\tau\), or certify an absolute objective gap without additional scalar information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding an arbitrary constant leaves all subgradient-only observations unchanged, making absolute values, fixed targets, and absolute gaps unidentifiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Constant Indistinguishability
Subgradient-Only Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact supporting subgradient information without usable objective-value information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and query domain \(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), a subgradient-only oracle maps each \(x\in Q\) to some \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), so
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
No exact or consistently comparable value of \(f(x)\) is returned. Consequently, oracle-based procedures cannot use objective-value comparisons or stopping tests requiring observed objective gaps unless separate value information is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns an exact subgradient but no dependable objective value, excluding value comparisons and objective-gap stopping tests based solely on its responses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical interface is coherent and fits the leaf, but the absence of any source prevents candidate-review acceptance of the oracle model and its information limitations.

children.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Oracle
children.top_down_role: Controlled deterministic relaxation of exact subgradient access.

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively relaxed supporting-hyperplane information for a convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). An \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient oracle returns a vector \(g_x\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\), meaning
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The set of all such vectors is the \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\). When \(\varepsilon=0\), this model reduces to exact subgradient access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns a supporting slope whose global subgradient inequality may fail by at most a prescribed additive tolerance epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_x\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\quad\forall y

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epsilon-subgradient definition is mathematically standard and correctly delimited, but it has no authoritative section, definition, or page citation.

children.title: Deterministically Inexact Oracle
children.top_down_role: Value or first-order information affected by bounded, relative, or vanishing deterministic error.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministically Inexact Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint convex oracle with explicitly bounded deterministic value and supporting-plane errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For convex \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) on a convex query domain \(Q\), a deterministically inexact oracle with tolerances \(\delta_v,\delta_g\ge0\) returns \((\widetilde f_x,\widetilde g_x)\) at \(x\in Q\) such that
\[
|\widetilde f_x-f(x)|\le\delta_v,
\qquad
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\widetilde g_x,y-x\rangle-\delta_g
\quad\text{for every }y\in Q.
\]
The tolerances may depend deterministically on the query or iteration; bounded, relative, and vanishing-error regimes arise by specifying corresponding bounds on these tolerance sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns approximate values and slopes whose deterministic value error and supporting-plane defect obey declared bounds, possibly varying or vanishing by iteration.
assumptions_latex: f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is convex on the convex domain }Q

notation.meaning: deterministic value and subgradient error bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated two-tolerance model is internally coherent, but deterministic inexact-oracle conventions vary. A source is required to establish this particular value-error and supporting-plane-error interface and its bounded, relative, and vanishing variants.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conservative Cut Under the Two-Tolerance Convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional consequence of the noncanonical deterministic-error convention in the deferred seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(|\widetilde f_x-f(x)|\le\delta_v\) and \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\widetilde g_x,y-x\rangle-\delta_g\) for every \(y\in Q\). Then \[m_x(y):=\widetilde f_x+\langle\widetilde g_x,y-x\rangle-(\delta_v+\delta_g)\] satisfies \(m_x(y)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the seed's two-tolerance convention, lowering the returned affine model by the sum of the errors gives a valid minorant.
knowledge_statements.title: Conservative Cut Under the Two-Tolerance Convention

Only a conditional corrected-minorant consequence is retained; exact, epsilon-only, and subgradient-only interfaces are excluded as siblings, while method-specific convergence and approximate projection access are excluded as downstream or separate scopes.

children.title: Euclidean Projection Oracle
children.top_down_role: Best-approximation access used by projected subgradient methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projection Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact best-approximation access to a nonempty closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. The Euclidean projection oracle accepts \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and returns the unique point
\[
P_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\frac12\|u-z\|_2^2.
\]
Its output is characterized by \(\langle z-P_C(z),u-P_C(z)\rangle\le0\) for every \(u\in C\). Thus a projected subgradient step with trial point \(z=x-\alpha g\) obtains the feasible update \(P_C(z)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given any Euclidean point, the oracle returns its unique nearest point in the nonempty closed convex feasible set.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Euclidean projection and proximality p. 73

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Euclidean projection and proximality p. 73

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failures when closedness or convexity is dropped.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(z=0\), the distance infimum is zero but no projection exists. For \(C=\{-1,1\}\) and \(z=0\), both points are nearest, so the projection is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed set can have no nearest point, while a nonconvex closed set can have several nearest points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Without closedness or convexity, }P_C\text{ need not be a single-valued everywhere-defined map.}
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Existence and Uniqueness Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core stability properties of exact Euclidean projection responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \[\|P_Cz-P_Cw\|_2^2\le\langle P_Cz-P_Cw,z-w\rangle.\] Hence \(P_C\) is nonexpansive. Moreover, for every \(u\in C\), \[\|P_Cz-u\|_2^2\le\|z-u\|_2^2-\|z-P_Cz\|_2^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact Euclidean projection is firmly nonexpansive and decreases squared distance to every feasible comparison point.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness and Fejér Inequality

children.title: Bregman Prox Oracle
children.top_down_role: Geometry-dependent feasible-set access used by mirror methods.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman Prox Variational Inequality and Three-Point Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order certificate for a Bregman prox output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the well-posedness assumptions, \(u^+\in C\) is the Bregman prox output if and only if \[\langle \eta g+\nabla h(u^+)-\nabla h(x),u-u^+\rangle\ge0\qquad(\forall u\in C).\] Consequently, for every \(u\in C\), \[\eta\langle g,u^+-u\rangle\le D_h(u,x)-D_h(u,u^+)-D_h(u^+,x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The prox variational inequality exactly certifies the output and yields the Bregman three-point inequality.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
h\text{ is differentiable and strongly convex on an open convex set containing }C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u^+=\operatorname{Prox}^{h}_{C}(x,\eta g)\iff \langle\eta g+\nabla h(u^+)-\nabla h(x),u-u^+\rangle\ge0\quad\forall u\in C
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Prox Variational Inequality and Three-Point Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failures of uniqueness or attainment after removing defining assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\equiv0\), \(C=[0,1]\), and \(g=0\), every \(u\in C\) minimizes the prox objective. If \(C=(0,1)\), \(h(u)=\tfrac12u^2\), \(x=\tfrac12\), \(\eta=1\), and \(g=\tfrac12\), the prox objective has derivative \(u\); its infimum is approached as \(u\downarrow0\) but is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strong convexity the output may be nonunique, and without closedness a strongly convex prox objective may not attain its infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Loss of strong convexity can destroy uniqueness, and loss of closedness can destroy attainment.}
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Prox Well-Posedness Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Uniqueness of the Bregman Prox Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-posedness of the exact Bregman prox query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose \(h\) is differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on an open convex set containing \(C\), where \(\mu>0\). For every \(x\in C\), \(g\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\eta>0\), the function \(u\mapsto\langle g,u\rangle+\eta^{-1}D_h(u,x)\) is strongly convex and coercive on \(C\), and therefore has a unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity of the reference function and closedness of the feasible set give a unique attained Bregman prox output.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
h\text{ is differentiable and }\mu\text{-strongly convex on an open convex set containing }C

notation.meaning: strong-convexity modulus of the reference function

knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Uniqueness of the Bregman Prox Output
Bregman Prox Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry-dependent prox access generated by a differentiable strongly convex reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(h\) be differentiable and strongly convex on a convex domain containing \(C\). Define \(D_h(u,x):=h(u)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),u-x\rangle\). Given \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), direction \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\eta>0\), the Bregman prox oracle returns
\[
\operatorname{Prox}^{h}_{C}(x,\eta g):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\left\{\langle g,u\rangle+\eta^{-1}D_h(u,x)\right\}.
\]
Strong convexity makes the returned minimizer unique whenever it exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle minimizes a linearized objective plus a Bregman-distance penalty over the feasible set, using geometry induced by a strongly convex reference function.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
h\text{ is differentiable and strongly convex on a domain containing }C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated linearized Bregman prox interface is a coherent convention and the conditional uniqueness claim is correct, but no authoritative locator supports the chosen normalization or assumptions.

children.title: Constraint Value–Subgradient Oracle
children.top_down_role: Functional-constraint access used by switching and penalty schemes.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Value–Subgradient Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint value and subgradient access for convex functional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex on a convex query domain \(C\). A constraint value–subgradient oracle accepts \(x\in C\) and an index \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and returns \((g_i(x),s_i)\) with \(s_i\in\partial g_i(x)\). Hence
\[
g_i(y)\ge g_i(x)+\langle s_i,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
The sign of \(g_i(x)\) tests the queried inequality \(g_i(x)\le0\), while \(s_i\) supplies a separating or corrective direction when the constraint is violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a selected convex inequality, the oracle returns its exact value and a subgradient, enabling feasibility tests and corrective subgradient steps.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.1 The convex constrained case p. 324

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.1 The convex constrained case p. 324

children.title: Regularity-Scale Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Regularity and size regimes used to classify the reach of convergence and complexity results.

children.title: Uniform Lipschitz Regime
children.top_down_role: Uniformly controlled oracle magnitude on the working domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Lipschitz Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform boundedness of convex subgradients throughout the working domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex and let \(f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. The uniform Lipschitz regime with constant \(G<\infty\) holds when every subgradient used by the oracle satisfies \(\|g\|_2\le G\) at every query point, or, in the intrinsic exact form, \(\sup\{\|g\|_2:g\in\partial f(x),\ x\in Q\}\le G\). The intrinsic bound implies
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in Q.
\]
Thus one finite scale controls all first-order oracle magnitudes on \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single finite constant bounds all relevant subgradient norms over the working domain and consequently bounds objective variation linearly with distance.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Fundamentals of the Theory and Methods of Unconstrained Minimization p. 2

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Fundamentals of the Theory and Methods of Unconstrained Minimization p. 2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Normals Break the Ambient Full-Subdifferential Converse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating relative Lipschitz continuity from ambient extended-value subgradient boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q=[0,\infty) and f(x)=0 on Q. Relative to Q, f is 0-Lipschitz. Its extended-value realization \bar f=f+\delta_Q satisfies \partial\bar f(0)=N_Q(0)=(-\infty,0], which is unbounded. Thus relative Lipschitz continuity on a closed constrained domain does not imply boundedness of every ambient subgradient at boundary points; an oracle-selection or relative-subdifferential convention must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant function on a half-line is Lipschitz, while its extended-value subdifferential is unbounded at the boundary because of outward normals.

notation.meaning: ambient convex normal cone to Q at zero

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Normals Break the Ambient Full-Subdifferential Converse

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence without constrained-boundary normal directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d be open and convex and let f:Q\to\mathbb R be convex. For G\ge0, the following are equivalent: \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2\quad\forall x,y\in Q,\] and \[\|g\|_2\le G\quad\forall x\in Q,\ \forall g\in\partial f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite convex function on an open convex domain, global G-Lipschitz continuity is equivalent to every convex subgradient having norm at most G.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is open and convex}.
f:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and finite-valued}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }G\text{-Lipschitz on }Q\Longleftrightarrow \sup_{x\in Q}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_2\le G.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Lipschitz–Subgradient Equivalence

children.title: Bounded-Region Regularity
children.top_down_role: Control available only on a relevant level set, comparison region, or feasible domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Bounded Region Need Not Bound Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-boundary pathology showing that geometric boundedness of the query region is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the proper closed convex function \[f(x)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt{x},&x\ge0,\\+\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}\] On the bounded region \(R=(0,1]\), \(f\) is differentiable and \[\partial f(x)=\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right\}.\] Hence \[\sup_{x\in R}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}|g|=+\infty.\] Thus boundedness of a region approaching the effective-domain boundary does not itself supply a finite regional subgradient constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded query region can have unbounded gradients as it approaches the boundary of a convex function's domain.

notation.meaning: bounded region approaching the effective-domain boundary

knowledge_statements.title: A Bounded Region Need Not Bound Subgradients

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Automatic Control on Compact Interior Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local boundedness of convex subgradients on compact subsets of the domain interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every compact set \(K\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists \(G_K<\infty\) such that \[\sup_{x\in K}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_2\le G_K.\] Consequently, bounded-region regularity follows once all relevant points are known to remain in such a compact interior region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradients are uniformly bounded on every compact set lying strictly inside the effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: compact interior region containing relevant points

knowledge_statements.title: Automatic Control on Compact Interior Regions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of uniform Lipschitz control and uniform full-subdifferential bounds on an open convex region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(U\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) be nonempty, open, and convex. For \(G\ge0\), the following are equivalent: \[(i)\quad |f(y)-f(x)|\le G\|y-x\|_2\quad\text{for all }x,y\in U;\] \[(ii)\quad \|g\|_2\le G\quad\text{for all }x\in U\text{ and }g\in\partial f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex region inside the effective domain, bounding every convex subgradient is equivalent to Lipschitz continuity with the same constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(U\) is nonempty, open, convex, and contained in \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }G\text{-Lipschitz on }U\iff\sup_{x\in U}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_2\le G.
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Lipschitz–Subgradient Equivalence
Bounded-Region Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local bounded-subgradient condition on the region containing all relevant iterates and comparison points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(R\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) be the region relevant to an algorithm. Bounded-region regularity holds on \(R\) with constant \(G<\infty\) when
\[\sup_{x\in R}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_2\le G.\]
If the oracle selects only one subgradient at each query, the weaker oracle-relative condition is \(\|g(x)\|_2\le G\) for every queried \(x\in R\). Complexity conclusions using \(G\) require the analyzed iterates and comparison points to remain in \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients need only be bounded on a region known to contain the analyzed iterates and comparison points; leaving that region invalidates bounds using the local constant.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) contains every relevant query and comparison point.

notation.meaning: region on which regularity is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and its condition content kind fit the bounded-region leaf, and the distinction between bounding the full subdifferential and bounding oracle-selected responses is mathematically meaningful. No source with a specific inspectable locator is supplied for the regional regularity formulation or its complexity boundary.

children.title: Solution-Relative Radius Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity organized through distance or divergence from the initial point to a solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Solution Radius Does Not Control Domain or Oracle Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of the solution-relative scale from sibling regularity scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For f(x)=x^2 on C=\mathbb R with x_0=1, the solution set is X^*=\{0\} and R_*=1. Nevertheless, C has infinite diameter and the unique subgradient g(x)=2x is unbounded on C. Hence a finite solution-relative radius alone implies neither bounded-region regularity nor a uniform oracle bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A starting point can be finitely far from a solution although the feasible region and global oracle magnitudes are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Solution Radius Does Not Control Domain or Oracle Size

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-Euclidean analogue of initial distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h be convex on a convex domain containing x_0 and a nonempty solution set X^*, and suppose h is differentiable at x_0. Define D_h(x,x_0)=h(x)-h(x_0)-\langle\nabla h(x_0),x-x_0\rangle and \[\mathcal R_{h,*}:=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}D_h(x^*,x_0).\] A mirror or dual-averaging analysis is divergence-radius controlled when it assumes a finite bound \(\mathcal R_h\ge\mathcal R_{h,*}\). For h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2, \(\mathcal R_{h,*}=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The non-Euclidean initial scale is the least Bregman divergence from the starting point to a solution; squared Euclidean distance is its quadratic special case.
assumptions_latex: h\text{ is convex on a domain containing }x_0\text{ and }X^*.

notation.meaning: least initial Bregman divergence to the solution set

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Relative Bregman Radius
Solution-Relative Radius Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean scale condition measured from initialization to a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\). Given \(x_0\in C\), the solution-relative radius is
\[R_*:=\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}\|x_0-x^*\|_2.\]
The problem is in a radius-controlled regime when analysis assumes or derives a finite upper bound \(R\ge R_*\). Such a bound controls only the initial distance to the solution set; it does not by itself bound the feasible-set diameter, later iterates, or oracle subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scale parameter is the distance from the initial point to the solution set, not the feasible-set diameter or a subgradient bound.

notation.meaning: distance from initialization to the solution set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-relative distance is precisely defined and the condition content kind fits the regime leaf. A source with a specific locator is required to support its use as the organizing scale in subgradient complexity analysis.

children.title: Unbounded-Oracle Regime
children.top_down_role: Problems outside uniform bounded-subgradient complexity models.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Oracle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of complexity analyses requiring a uniform bound on returned subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a subgradient oracle for a proper convex function \(f\) return \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\) at queried points. The oracle is outside the uniform bounded-subgradient model on a query region \(R\) when no finite \(G\) satisfies
\[\|g(x)\|_2\le G\quad\text{for every admissible query }x\in R.\]
For example, \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) has the unique subgradient \(g(x)=2x\), which is unbounded on \(R=\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, a convergence or complexity bound whose hypotheses require a global finite \(G\) cannot be invoked without additionally proving bounded iterates or replacing that hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If oracle responses are not uniformly bounded on admissible queries, standard bounds parameterized by a global subgradient constant do not apply without localization or new assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\) at each admissible query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in R}\|g(x)\|_2=+\infty\), so results requiring a finite uniform oracle bound are inapplicable.

notation.meaning: oracle-selected subgradient at the query point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary content kind matches the leaf, and the quadratic example correctly demonstrates failure of a global bounded-oracle hypothesis. No authoritative source with a specific locator supports the stated model boundary and complexity consequence.

children.title: Oracle Representation Links
children.top_down_role: Structural links between subgradients, affine minorants, and separation information.

children.title: Subgradient-Minorant Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The affine-minorant interpretation of convex subgradient information.

children.title: Subgradient Information
children.top_down_role: Objective-oracle information represented by a selected convex subgradient.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order information for a proper convex objective at one domain point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A vector \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) precisely when
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
The subdifferential is \(\partial f(x):=\{g: g\text{ satisfies this inequality}\}\). Thus exact subgradient information at \(x\) consists of the value \(f(x)\) together with at least one vector \(g\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient is a vector whose affine first-order model globally underestimates the convex objective; an exact oracle supplies the value and such a vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for all \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the objective at the query point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex subgradient definition is mathematically standard and the definition content kind fits the leaf. The record provides no authoritative definition or oracle-model citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Supporting Affine Minorants
children.top_down_role: Global affine lower models associated with convex objective information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of a supporting affine minorant as a supporting hyperplane of the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(m(y)=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\). Then \(m\) is a supporting affine minorant of \(f\) at \(x\) if and only if \[\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\{(y,t):t\ge m(y)\}\] and the boundary hyperplane \(t=m(y)\) contains \((x,f(x))\). Equivalently, \((g,-1)\) is normal to a hyperplane supporting \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A touching affine minorant is exactly a nonvertical supporting hyperplane of the function's epigraph.

notation.meaning: normal to the supporting epigraph hyperplane

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Supporting-Hyperplane Representation
Supporting Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine global underestimators that touch a convex function at the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). An affine function \(m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is a supporting affine minorant of \(f\) at \(x\) when
\[m(y)\le f(y)\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad m(x)=f(x).\]
Every such affine function can be written as \(m(y)=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for some slope \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\); the global-minorant condition then determines whether that slope supports \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting affine minorant is an affine global lower bound that equals the convex objective at its support point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\) supports \(f\) at \(x\) exactly when \(m\le f\) globally and \(m(x)=f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of a touching affine global minorant is precise and fits the terminal container. The claim that every such affine function has the displayed value-slope form is standard, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Oracle-to-Minorant Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between subgradient oracle outputs and supporting lower models.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-to-Minorant Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between a convex subgradient response and a touching affine lower model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Define
\[m_{x,g}(y):=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle.\]
Then
\[g\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m_{x,g}(y)\le f(y)\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Moreover, \(m_{x,g}(x)=f(x)\). Hence an exact oracle response \((f(x),g)\) determines a supporting affine minorant, while the value and slope of any supporting affine minorant at \(x\) recover an exact subgradient response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value–subgradient pair and a touching affine global minorant encode exactly the same local oracle information for a convex objective.

notation.meaning: affine model generated by the value–subgradient pair

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind correctly captures the exact equivalence between a subgradient response and its touching affine minorant. The mathematical statement is precise, but it lacks an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Minorant Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of the affine-minorant interpretation across oracle types or objective classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limits on recovering an exact global subgradient from an affine lower model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\), an affine function \(m(y)=a+\langle g,y\rangle\) that satisfies \(m\le f\) globally and \(m(x)=f(x)\) encodes \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Neither condition can be discarded as an inference rule. For \(f(y)=e^y\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(m(y)=0\) is a strict global affine minorant, but its slope \(0\) belongs to no \(\partial f(x)=\{e^x\}\). For \(f(y)=y^2\), the affine function \(m(y)=-y\) satisfies \(m(y)\le f(y)\) on \([0,\infty)\) and touches at \(0\), but its slope \(-1\notin\partial f(0)=\{0\}\) because the minorant is not globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minorant without contact and a touching minorant valid only on a restricted set need not encode any exact global subgradient at the proposed point.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\le f\text{ globally and }m(x)=f(x)\Longrightarrow \nabla m\in\partial f(x),\text{ while either condition alone is insufficient.}
knowledge_statements.title: Contact and Global-Validity Boundaries
Minorant Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of recovering exact subgradient information from arbitrary affine lower models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. An affine global minorant \(m(y)=a+\langle g,y\rangle\) need not encode a subgradient at a specified point \(x\): recovery requires the contact condition \(m(x)=f(x)\). For example, for \(f(y)=y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the affine function \(m(y)=-1\) satisfies \(m(y)\le f(y)\) everywhere but touches nowhere and therefore yields no pair \((x,g)\) with \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Likewise, an affine model valid only on a restricted set does not generally certify a global convex subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontouching or merely local affine lower bound does not determine an exact global subgradient; global validity and contact are both essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without both \(m\le f\) globally and \(m(x)=f(x)\), the slope of \(m\) need not belong to \(\partial f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary content kind fits the representation-boundaries leaf, and the nontouching-minorant counterexample is correct. No source with a specific locator supports the stated global-validity and contact boundary.

children.title: Subgradient-Separation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The bridge from objective information to separating hyperplanes for suitable level sets.

children.title: Objective Subgradient Information
children.top_down_role: Subgradient information supplied through objective evaluation channels.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value and subgradient response used to derive objective level-set cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Exact objective subgradient information at \(x\) is a pair \((f(x),g)\) with \(g\in\partial f(x)\), meaning
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Given a target level \(\alpha<f(x)\), this information implies a linear inequality satisfied by every point in the lower level set \(L_\alpha:=\{y:f(y)\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact objective information consists of the queried value and a subgradient; together they imply a valid halfspace containing every point below a chosen target level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f(x),g)\) is exact objective subgradient information when \(g\in\partial f(x)\).

notation.meaning: objective lower level set at level alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the objective-information leaf, and the value-subgradient pair is correctly specified. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied for the exact objective oracle formulation or its level-set implication.

children.title: Level-Set Separation
children.top_down_role: Separating-hyperplane information associated with suitable objective level sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halfspace certificate separating an infeasible query from a convex lower level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, fix \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and define \(L_\alpha:=\{y:f(y)\le\alpha\}\). For a query \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(f(x)>\alpha\), a vector \(g\ne0\) supplies a strict level-set separation certificate when
\[\langle g,y-x\rangle\le\alpha-f(x)<0\quad\text{for every }y\in L_\alpha.\]
The displayed inequality is verifiable from a valid subgradient inequality and certifies that \(L_\alpha\) lies in a closed halfspace that excludes \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector separates a query above the target value from the lower level set when every lower-level point lies strictly beyond the induced hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha\subseteq\{y:\langle g,y-x\rangle\le\alpha-f(x)\}\) and \(x\) is excluded from this halfspace.

children.title: Subgradient-to-Separation Bridge
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from objective subgradients to level-set separators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative geometry of the separator generated by a nonzero objective subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper and convex, let \(g\in\partial f(x)\), and suppose \(L_\alpha:=\{y:f(y)\le\alpha\}\neq\varnothing\) with \(\alpha<f(x)\). Then \(g\neq0\), and for \[H_{x,g,\alpha}:=\{y:\langle g,y-x\rangle\le\alpha-f(x)\}\] one has \[\operatorname{dist}(x,H_{x,g,\alpha})=\frac{f(x)-\alpha}{\|g\|_2}.\] Since \(L_\alpha\subseteq H_{x,g,\alpha}\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,L_\alpha)\ge\frac{f(x)-\alpha}{\|g\|_2}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient separator has an explicit normalized margin, giving a lower bound on the query's distance from the lower level set.

notation.meaning: halfspace generated by the exact value–subgradient response
Euclidean distance from x to a set S

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Margin and Distance Bound
Subgradient-to-Separation Bridge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an objective subgradient response into a lower-level-set separating cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(g\in\partial f(x)\), and choose \(\alpha<f(x)\). For every \(y\in L_\alpha:=\{z:f(z)\le\alpha\}\), the subgradient inequality gives
\[\langle g,y-x\rangle\le f(y)-f(x)\le\alpha-f(x)<0.\]
Thus the oracle response \((f(x),g)\) generates the valid separating halfspace
\[H_{x,g,\alpha}:=\{y:\langle g,y-x\rangle\le\alpha-f(x)\},\qquad L_\alpha\subseteq H_{x,g,\alpha},\quad x\notin H_{x,g,\alpha}.\]
If \(L_\alpha\neq\varnothing\), these inequalities also imply \(g\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point above the target level, a convex subgradient directly yields a halfspace containing the entire lower level set and excluding the query.

notation.meaning: halfspace generated by the oracle response and target level

children.title: Separation Interface Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where objective information does not furnish the required separation access.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Nonconvex Derivatives Need Not Separate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the global level-set cut when convexity and global affine support are absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(t)=-|t|\), take \(x=1\), \(\alpha=-2\), and \(g=f'(1)=-1\). Then \(f(x)=-1>\alpha\) and \[L_\alpha=(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty).\] The convex bridge formula gives \[H=\{y:-(y-1)\le-1\}=[2,\infty),\] which omits the branch \(( -\infty,-2]\) of \(L_\alpha\). Thus a local derivative without a global convex support inequality need not produce a valid level-set separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconvex objective, even an ordinary derivative at a point above the target level can generate a halfspace that cuts off part of the lower level set.

notation.meaning: halfspace obtained by applying the convex bridge formula

knowledge_statements.title: Local Nonconvex Derivatives Need Not Separate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp query-position and nonemptiness requirements for meaningful strict level-set separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_\alpha=\{y:f(y)\le\alpha\}\). If \(f(x)\le\alpha\), then \(x\in L_\alpha\), so no halfspace can both contain \(L_\alpha\) and exclude \(x\). If \(L_\alpha=\varnothing\), containment in any halfspace is vacuous; a returned halfspace therefore does not certify nontrivial geometric separation from an existing target set, and target containment alone does not force a nonzero normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation requires the query to lie above the target level, while separation of an empty lower level set is vacuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\le\alpha\Rightarrow x\in L_\alpha;\qquad L_\alpha=\varnothing\Rightarrow L_\alpha\subseteq H\text{ is vacuous for every }H.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold and Empty-Level Degeneracies

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact error threshold under which an epsilon-subgradient still strictly excludes the query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper and convex, let \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\), and let \(\alpha<f(x)\). Then every \(y\in L_\alpha\) satisfies \[\langle g,y-x\rangle\le\alpha-f(x)+\varepsilon.\] Hence \(L_\alpha\) lies in the resulting closed halfspace. That halfspace excludes \(x\) exactly when \[\varepsilon<f(x)-\alpha.\] At equality it contains \(x\), and for larger error this response does not furnish strict separation by the displayed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient gives a strict level-set separator only when its error is smaller than the objective gap above the target level.

notation.meaning: halfspace generated by the approximate response

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Subgradient Separation Threshold
Separation Interface Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lost when replacing objective oracle responses by level-set separating cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separating halfspace for one lower level set generally does not recover exact objective subgradient information. For \(f_1(t)=t\) and \(f_2(t)=2t\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), take \(x=1\) and \(\alpha=0\). Both lower level sets equal \(( -\infty,0]\), and the halfspace \(H=( -\infty,0]\) separates \(x\) from either set, yet the exact responses are \((f_1(1),1)=(1,1)\) and \((f_2(1),2)=(2,2)\). Thus a separation oracle may omit objective values, subgradient magnitudes, and information about other levels; the subgradient-to-separation map is not generally invertible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level-set cut is weaker than an exact value–subgradient response: different objectives and subgradients can produce the same separating halfspace.
assumptions_latex: The interface returns only a halfspace containing a specified lower level set and excluding the query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Level-set separation data do not generally determine \(f(x)\) or a unique element of \(\partial f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary content kind fits the leaf, and the two linear objectives correctly show that identical level-set separation data need not determine objective values or subgradient magnitudes. children.title: Subgradient Method
children.top_down_role: The foundational Euclidean method family for unconstrained nonsmooth convex minimization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local distance reduction by a normalized negative subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step strict distance reduction for finite-valued unconstrained convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and let \[S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\neq\varnothing.\] If \(x_k\notin S^*\), then for every \(x^*\in S^*\) and every \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), there exists \(T_k>0\) such that, for every \(\alpha\in(0,T_k)\), \[\left\lVert x_k-\alpha\frac{g_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}-x^*\right\rVert_2<\lVert x_k-x^*\rVert_2.\] Under these assumptions, the selected \(g_k\) is necessarily nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any nonoptimal point of a convex function with a minimizer, every selected subgradient admits a positive threshold such that all smaller normalized negative-subgradient steps strictly reduce the distance to any chosen minimizer.

children.title: Standard Subgradient Form
children.top_down_role: The classical current-oracle-response Euclidean trajectory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical raw exact-subgradient trajectory without projection or normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\eta_k>0\). At iteration \(k\), select \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), stop: \(x_k\) minimizes \(f\). Otherwise set \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply the current exact subgradient by a positive stepsize and subtract it, stopping when the selected subgradient is zero.

notation.meaning: Multiplier applied to the raw subgradient.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Standard Subgradient Form
Standard Subgradient Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected Euclidean subgradient iteration using the current exact oracle response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a proper convex objective \(f\), an initial point \(x_0\in C\), positive stepsizes \((\eta_k)_{k\ge0}\), and an iteration limit \(T\). For \(k=0,\ldots,T-1\), query an exact oracle for any \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and update
\[x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_k g_k),\qquad \Pi_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|x-z\|_2.\]
Stop after \(T\) updates. Output either the last iterate \(x_T\) or the stepsize-weighted average \(\bar x_T:=\bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_kx_k\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_k\bigr)\), according to the stated convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, move opposite a current subgradient, project onto the feasible set, and return either the final iterate or a specified weighted average.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex with \(\partial f(x_k)\neq\varnothing\) at every query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_k g_k)\) with \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), followed by the prescribed last-iterate or averaged output.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind exactly fits the standard subgradient-form leaf, and the projected update is well defined under the stated assumptions. An authoritative algorithm citation with a specific section, theorem, or page locator is missing, including support for the stated output alternatives.

children.title: Normalized Subgradient Form
children.top_down_role: A displacement-normalized Euclidean variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Subgradient Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Euclidean subgradient iteration with prescribed displacement length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and positive step lengths \((\alpha_k)_{k\ge 0}\). At iteration \(k\), select \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), stop and output \(x_k\), which minimizes \(f\). Otherwise set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\frac{g_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}.
\]
Thus every nonzero displacement has Euclidean length \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert_2=\alpha_k\), independently of the selected subgradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move opposite a chosen subgradient after normalizing it, so the prescribed parameter equals the Euclidean displacement length; stop when the subgradient is zero.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x
selected subgradient at the current iterate

children.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Method
children.top_down_role: The classical method family corresponding to relaxed subgradient information.

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Euclidean method using additively relaxed convex subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Given \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and tolerances \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), choose \(g_k\in\partial_{\varepsilon_k}f(x_k)\), meaning
\[
f(y)\ge f(x_k)+\langle g_k,y-x_k\rangle-\varepsilon_k\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Update
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.
\]
After a prescribed iteration budget, output either the final iterate or an explicitly chosen best or weighted-average iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iterate, use a vector satisfying the subgradient inequality up to additive error, then take an ordinary subgradient displacement.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Direct Methods p. 87

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Direct Methods p. 87

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon and asymptotic guarantees with additive subgradient errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), choose \(x^*\in X^*\), and suppose \(\|g_k\|_2\le G\). For \(S_T=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k\) and \(\bar x_T=S_T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_kx_k\), \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le\frac{\|x_0-x^*\|_2^2+G^2\sum_{k<T}\alpha_k^2+2\sum_{k<T}\alpha_k\varepsilon_k}{2S_T}.\] Consequently \(f(\bar x_T)\to f^*\) if \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual ergodic subgradient bound gains a weighted additive-error term.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex and has a minimizer \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Ergodic Bound

children.title: Projected Subgradient Method
children.top_down_role: The canonical Euclidean method family for simple convex constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence under Polyak steps and under diminishing nonsummable steps with uniformly bounded selected subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex, let $Q$ be closed and convex, and suppose $X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}f(x)\neq\varnothing$. For $g_k\in\partial f(x^k)$ and
\[
x^{k+1}=P_Q(x^k-\gamma_k g_k),
\]
the choice
\[
\gamma_k=\frac{f(x^k)-f^*}{\|g_k\|^2},\qquad f^*=\min_{x\in Q}f(x),
\]
yields $x^k\to x^*\in X^*$. If the selected subgradients are uniformly bounded on $Q$, then
\[
\gamma_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_k=\infty
\]
also yields $x^k\to x^*\in X^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected subgradient converges to a constrained minimizer with Polyak steps. Diminishing nonsummable steps also converge when the selected subgradients are uniformly bounded on Q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_k=\frac{f(x^k)-f^*}{\|g_k\|^2}\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*\in X^*;\qquad \bigl(\|g_k\|\le c,\ \gamma_k\to0,\ \sum_k\gamma_k=\infty\bigr)\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*\in X^*

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient minimization of a convex function over a set admitting metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex function $f$, select $g_k\in\partial f(x^k)$ and update
\[
x^{k+1}=P_Q(x^k-\gamma_k g_k).

The stated stepsize alternatives are
\[
\gamma_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_k=\infty,

\[
\gamma_k=\frac{f(x^k)-f^*}{\|g_k\|^2},\qquad f^*=\min_{x\in Q}f(x).

children.title: Direct Projected Subgradient

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Projected Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient iteration for minimizing a convex function over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex with available subgradients on \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\). Choose \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha_k>0\). At iteration \(k\), select \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and compute
\[
x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k),\qquad P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\lVert x-z\rVert_2.
\]
Stop by a prescribed budget or residual rule and output a specified final, best, or averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a subgradient step and project the displaced point onto the closed convex feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex with \(\partial f(x_k)\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Affine-Set Projection Regime
children.top_down_role: Projected subgradient schemes over affine feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nullspace Form of the Affine Projected Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of affine-set projected motion to the feasible nullspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\), \(x_k\in C\), and \(\Pi_{\ker A}=I-A^{\mathsf T}(AA^{\mathsf T})^\dagger A\). Then \[P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)=x_k-\alpha_k\Pi_{\ker A}g_k.\] Thus only the tangent component of the subgradient moves the iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a feasible point, affine projection removes the row-space component of the subgradient direction.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the nullspace of A

knowledge_statements.title: Nullspace Form of the Affine Projected Step
Affine-Set Projection Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Euclidean projection onto a consistent system of affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\) be nonempty, where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). For every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean projection onto \(C\) is
\[
P_C(z)=z-A^{\mathsf T}(AA^{\mathsf T})^\dagger(Az-b),
\]
where \((AA^{\mathsf T})^\dagger\) is the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. If \(A\) has full row rank, this reduces to
\[
P_C(z)=z-A^{\mathsf T}(AA^{\mathsf T})^{-1}(Az-b).
\]
Consequently, a projected subgradient step over \(C\) can be implemented by solving a linear system in the constraint space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto consistent affine equalities is obtained by correcting the point in the row space using a pseudoinverse or linear solve.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the affine set C

children.title: Conic-Set Projection Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and multiplier characterization for an affine slice of a cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. The projection \(p=P_C(z)\) is the unique minimizer of \(\frac12\|x-z\|^2\) over \(C\) and satisfies \(z-p\in N_C(p)\). If \(\operatorname{ri}K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\), this is equivalent to the existence of \(y\) and \(s\in N_K(p)\) such that \(z-p=A^{\mathsf T}y+s\), together with \(Ap=b\) and \(p\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a qualified affine conic slice is certified by feasibility and equality-plus-cone normal multipliers.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=P_C(z)\iff \exists y,\ s\in N_K(p):\ p\in K,\ Ap=b,\ z-p=A^{\mathsf T}y+s

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to K at p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical separable conic projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), \[(P_K(z))_i=\max\{z_i,0\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the nonnegative orthant clips negative coordinates to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative-Orthant Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form projection onto the Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(t,u):t\ge\|u\|\}\) and \(r=\|u\|\). Then \[P_K(t,u)=\begin{cases}(t,u),&r\le t,\\(0,0),&r\le-t,\\\frac{t+r}{2}(1,u/r),&|t|<r.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a second-order cone has an explicit three-case formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Projection
Conic-Set Projection Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto a closed convex cone via polar-cone decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and define its polar by \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). For every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), Moreau decomposition gives
\[
z=P_K(z)+P_{K^\circ}(z),\qquad \langle P_K(z),P_{K^\circ}(z)\rangle=0.
\]
Hence
\[
P_K(z)=z-P_{K^\circ}(z).
\]
A projected subgradient iteration over \(K\) may therefore compute \(x_{k+1}=P_K(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\) using either a primal-cone or polar-cone projection routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex cone is the component complementary and orthogonal to the projection onto its polar cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Projection Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle condition under which projected subgradient iterations are directly implementable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex feasible set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), structured projection access means that an algorithm can evaluate
\[
P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\lVert x-z\rVert_2^2
\]
for every queried \(z\), either exactly or with a declared error bound \(\lVert \widetilde P_C(z)-P_C(z)\rVert_2\le\delta\). Direct projected subgradient updates are executable under exact access by querying \(z_k=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\). Under inexact access, the update must explicitly use \(x_{k+1}=\widetilde P_C(z_k)\), and convergence guarantees require assumptions controlling the error sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection access supplies the nearest feasible point for each query, exactly or with a declared approximation error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(z)\) or \(\widetilde P_C(z)\) with \(\lVert\widetilde P_C(z)-P_C(z)\rVert_2\le\delta\) is available.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Direct Methods p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Persistent Projection Error Can Prevent Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that a uniform projection-error bound alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[0,\infty)\), \(f(x)=x\), and fix \(\delta>0\). Starting at \(x_0=\delta\), use \(g_k=1\), \(\alpha_k=\delta\), and an inexact oracle satisfying \(\widetilde P_C(0)=\delta\). This output is feasible and obeys \(|\widetilde P_C(0)-P_C(0)|=\delta\), yet \(x_k=\delta\) for every \(k\). Thus a nonvanishing absolute error allowance does not by itself preserve convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed admissible projection error can make projected subgradient iterations stall away from the optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Projection Error Can Prevent Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Rules for Structured Projection Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection access inherited by products and orthogonal images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), then \[P_C(z_1,\ldots,z_m)=(P_{C_1}(z_1),\ldots,P_{C_m}(z_m)).\] If \(Q\) is orthogonal and \(a\) is fixed, then \[P_{a+QC}(z)=a+QP_C(Q^{\mathsf T}(z-a)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Products project blockwise, while translated orthogonal images project by transforming to and from the original coordinates.
assumptions_latex: C_i\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for every }i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end accounting when every outer iteration invokes projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T\) projected-subgradient iterations each incur a subgradient cost \(C_g\) and projection cost \(C_P\), then, apart from vector overhead, the accumulated cost is \(T(C_g+C_P)\). Hence \(C_P\gg C_g\) makes projection dominate practical work even when outer oracle complexity remains \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expensive projection is paid at every outer iteration and can dominate total work.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection Projection Is Not One-Pass Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Obstruction to constructing an intersection projector from easy component projectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb R\}\), \(D=\{(s,s):s\in\mathbb R\}\), and \(z=(1,0)\). Although both projectors are elementary and \(C\cap D=\{0\}\), \[P_C(P_D(z))=(1/2,0)\ne(0,0)=P_{C\cap D}(z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even easily projected subspaces need not yield their intersection projector by one composition.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Projection Is Not One-Pass Composition
Structured Projection Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A simple feasible-set description need not imply inexpensive Euclidean projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Direct projected subgradient methods require solving a nearest-point problem at every iteration. This can be the dominant operation even when membership in the feasible set is easy. Concretely, for the positive-semidefinite cone \(C=\mathbb{S}_+^n\), a symmetric matrix \(Z=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)Q^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies
\[
P_C(Z)=Q\operatorname{diag}(\max\{\lambda_i,0\})Q^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus exact projection generally requires a spectral decomposition; for dense unstructured matrices its standard arithmetic cost is cubic in \(n\). Without an efficient exact or controlled-inexact projection routine, the nominally simple projected subgradient update is not computationally cheap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection can dominate each iteration; projection onto the semidefinite cone, for example, generally requires an eigenvalue decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(Z)=Q\operatorname{diag}(\max\{\lambda_i,0\})Q^{\mathsf T}\), requiring spectral computation in general.

notation.meaning: cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Projection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility iteration for one convex inequality using a supporting halfspace correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and suppose \(S=\{x:f(x)\le0\}\ne\varnothing\). Choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k\in(0,2)\). If \(f(x_k)\le0\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Otherwise choose a nonzero \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k\frac{f(x_k)}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2}g_k.
\]
The unrelaxed point is the Euclidean projection of \(x_k\) onto the supporting halfspace \(\{y:f(x_k)+\langle g_k,y-x_k\rangle\le0\}\). Stop when feasibility tolerance or iteration budget is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a convex inequality is violated, project toward its subgradient supporting halfspace; otherwise leave the iterate unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k f(x_k)g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2\) for a violated inequality.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Direct Methods p. 87

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Direct Methods p. 87

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance decrease and finite-dimensional convergence of relaxed supporting-halfspace corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x:f(x)\le0\}\ne\varnothing\) and apply the seed update. For every \(z\in S\), whenever \(f(x_k)>0\), \[\|x_{k+1}-z\|_2^2\le \|x_k-z\|_2^2-\lambda_k(2-\lambda_k)\frac{f(x_k)^2}{\|g_k\|_2^2}.\] Thus the trajectory is Fejer monotone with respect to \(S\). If \(\lambda_k\in[\delta,2-\delta]\) for some \(\delta>0\), then the finite-dimensional sequence converges to a point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every violated-constraint correction decreases distance to all feasible points; relaxation bounded away from zero and two yields convergence to feasibility.

notation.meaning: Uniform relaxation margin from zero and two.
