knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak convergence of intermittently controlled relaxed subgradient projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives weak convergence for relaxed subgradient projections onto finitely many consistent convex sublevel sets under bounded-intermittent control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of continuous convex functions \(f_i:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) with
\[
C=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{lev}_{\leq0}f_i\neq\varnothing.
\]
Assume either that every \(f_i\) is bounded on every bounded subset of \(\mathcal H\), that every \(f_i^*\) is supercoercive, or that \(\mathcal H\) is finite-dimensional. Suppose \(\mathrm i:\mathbb N\to I\) satisfies, for some integer \(m>0\),
\[
(\forall i\in I)(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\quad i\in\{\mathrm i(n),\ldots,\mathrm i(n+m-1)\}.
\]
For every \(i\), choose a selection \(s_i\) of \(\partial f_i\) and let \(G_i\) be the associated projector onto \(\operatorname{lev}_{\leq0}f_i\). If
\[
0<\inf_n\lambda_n\leq\sup_n\lambda_n<2,
\]
then, for every \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), the iteration
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(G_{\mathrm i(n)}x_n-x_n)
\]
converges weakly to a point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many consistent convex inequalities, relaxed subgradient projections converge weakly to a common feasible point when each inequality is selected at least once in every fixed-length window, the relaxation parameters remain uniformly separated from zero and two, and one of the stated boundedness, conjugate-supercoercivity, or finite-dimensionality conditions holds.
assumptions_latex: f_i:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex for every }i\in I
[(\forall i)\ f_i\text{ is bounded on bounded sets}]\lor[(\forall i)\ f_i^*\text{ is supercoercive}]\lor[\dim\mathcal H<\infty]
(\exists m\in\mathbb N_{>0})(\forall i\in I)(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ i\in\{\mathrm i(n),\ldots,\mathrm i(n+m-1)\}
s_i\text{ is a selection of }\partial f_i\text{ for every }i\in I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient projector onto a convex sublevel set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the subgradient projection associated with a continuous convex inequality in a Hilbert space, including its differentiable specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, let \(\xi\in\mathbb R\), and suppose \(C=\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\xi}f\neq\varnothing\). For a selection \(s\) of \(\partial f\), the associated subgradient projector is
\[
Gx=\begin{cases}
x+\dfrac{\xi-f(x)}{\lVert s(x)\rVert^2}s(x),&f(x)>\xi,\\
x,&f(x)\leq\xi.
\end{cases}
\]
The point \(Gx\) is the subgradient projection of \(x\) onto \(C\). If \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable on \(\mathcal H\setminus C\), then \(s(x)\) is replaced by \(\nabla f(x)\) in the branch \(f(x)>\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient projector fixes points in the nonempty convex sublevel set and moves each point outside it along a selected subgradient by the normalized sublevel violation. If the function is Gâteaux differentiable outside the set, the gradient defines the exterior branch.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
s\text{ is a selection of }\partial f
\text{For the gradient specialization, }f\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable on }\mathcal H\setminus C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gx=\begin{cases}x+(\xi-f(x))s(x)/\lVert s(x)\rVert^2,&f(x)>\xi,\\x,&f(x)\leq\xi,\end{cases}\quad\text{with }s(x)\text{ replaced by }\nabla f(x)\text{ in the differentiable specialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak convergence of Polyak's projected subgradient algorithm with known optimal value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States weak convergence of the projected Polyak subgradient iteration for constrained convex minimization when the optimal value is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a closed convex subset of \(\mathcal H\), let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, and suppose \(\operatorname{Argmin}_C f\neq\varnothing\). Assume either that \(f\) is bounded on every bounded subset of \(\mathcal H\), that \(f^*\) is supercoercive, or that \(\mathcal H\) is finite-dimensional. Let
\[
0<\inf_n\alpha_n\leq\sup_n\alpha_n<2,
\qquad \mu=\min_{x\in C}f(x),
\]
choose a selection \(s\) of \(\partial f\), and take \(x_0\in C\). Define
\[
x_{n+1}=\begin{cases}
P_C\!\left(x_n+\alpha_n\dfrac{\mu-f(x_n)}{\lVert s(x_n)\rVert^2}s(x_n)\right),&s(x_n)\neq0,\\
x_n,&s(x_n)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \((x_n)\) converges weakly to an element of \(\operatorname{Argmin}_C f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For constrained minimization of a continuous convex function with known optimal value, the projected Polyak subgradient iteration converges weakly to a constrained minimizer when the relaxation parameters remain uniformly separated from zero and two and one of the stated boundedness, conjugate-supercoercivity, or finite-dimensionality conditions holds. If the selected subgradient is zero, the iterate is left unchanged.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathcal H\text{ is closed and convex}
f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
f\text{ is bounded on bounded sets}\lor f^*\text{ is supercoercive}\lor\dim\mathcal H<\infty
s\text{ is a selection of }\partial f
\mu=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\text{ is known to the iteration}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and regularity of a subgradient projector
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the fixed-point, supporting-halfspace, residual, demiclosedness, and continuity properties of a subgradient projector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, let \(C=\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\xi}f\neq\varnothing\), let \(s\) be a selection of \(\partial f\), and let \(G\) be the associated subgradient projector. For \(x\in\mathcal H\), set
\[
H_x=\{y\in\mathcal H\mid \langle y-x,s(x)\rangle+f(x)\leq\xi\}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{Fix}G=C\subset H_x\), \(Gx=P_{H_x}x\), and \(G\) is firmly quasinonexpansive. Moreover,
\[
(f(x)-\xi)_+=\lVert s(x)\rVert\,\lVert Gx-x\rVert,
\qquad
(f(x)-\xi)_+(x-Gx)=\lVert Gx-x\rVert^2s(x).
\]
If \(Gx_n-x_n\to0\) and either \(x_n\to\bar x\), or \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\) while \(f\) is bounded on every bounded subset of \(\mathcal H\), then \(\bar x\in C\). Under the bounded-on-bounded-sets assumption, \(\operatorname{Id}-G\) is demiclosed at zero. The map \(G\) is continuous on \(C\); if \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(\mathcal H\setminus C\), then \(G\) is continuous on \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient projector is the metric projection of the current point onto its subgradient supporting halfspace, has the sublevel set as its fixed-point set, is firmly quasinonexpansive, and satisfies exact violation–residual identities. A strongly convergent sequence with vanishing projector residual has a feasible limit; the analogous weak conclusion and demiclosedness require boundedness of the function on bounded sets. The projector is continuous on the feasible set and is globally continuous under exterior Fréchet differentiability.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
s\text{ is a selection of }\partial f
G\text{ is the subgradient projector associated with }(f,\xi,s)
\text{Weak-limit and demiclosedness conclusions additionally require }f\text{ bounded on bounded subsets of }\mathcal H
\text{Global continuity additionally requires Fréchet differentiability on }\mathcal H\setminus C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Fix}G=C\subset H_x,\quad Gx=P_{H_x}x,\quad G\text{ is firmly quasinonexpansive, with the stated residual identities and conditional limit, demiclosedness, and continuity properties.}

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Stepsize Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard subgradient iteration with a fixed multiplier on the raw subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimizing a proper convex function \(f\) over a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), choose \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) and a constant \(\alpha>0\). At every iteration select \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and compute
\[
x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k).
\]
In the unconstrained case take \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), so \(P_C\) is the identity. Before projection, the displacement length is \(\alpha\lVert g_k\rVert_2\); hence a constant stepsize does not generally give a constant geometric step length. Stop after a prescribed budget and report a declared final, best, or averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply every raw subgradient by the same positive scalar; the resulting displacement still varies with the subgradient norm.

children.title: Constant Step-Length Policies

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Step-Length Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized projected subgradient iteration with fixed pre-projection displacement length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimizing a proper convex function \(f\) over a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), choose \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) and a fixed length \(\ell>0\). Select \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), stop and output \(x_k\). Otherwise compute
\[
x_{k+1}=P_C\!\left(x_k-\ell\frac{g_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}\right).
\]
The displacement before projection has length exactly \(\ell\), while nonexpansiveness of projection gives \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert_2\le\ell\). Stop after a prescribed budget if no zero subgradient occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize each nonzero subgradient and use a fixed displacement length; projection can only shorten the realized move.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Scale Neighborhood Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic objective neighborhoods for constant raw and normalized projected steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and suppose \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Choose \(x_0\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), and at every generated iterate choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) with \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\le G\). For the constant-stepsize iteration
\[
x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k),\qquad \alpha>0,
\]
one has
\[
\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\le f(x^*)+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}.
\]
For an infinite nonterminating sequence generated by the constant-step-length iteration
\[
x_{k+1}=P_C\!\left(x_k-\ell\frac{g_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}\right),\qquad \ell>0,
\]
where \(g_k\ne0\) for every \(k\), one has
\[
\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\le f(x^*)+\frac{\ell G}{2}.
\]
Thus a fixed positive scale guarantees repeated approach to a scale-dependent objective neighborhood, rather than exact asymptotic optimality in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For projected subgradient sequences with uniformly bounded selected subgradients, a fixed raw stepsize gives a liminf objective gap at most alpha times G squared over two. An infinite normalized fixed-length sequence gives a liminf gap at most the fixed length times G over two.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex and attains its minimum over \(C\).
For the normalized result, the generated sequence is infinite and \(g_k\ne0\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the raw policy, \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\le f^*+\alpha G^2/2\); for the normalized policy, \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\le f^*+\ell G/2\).

notation.meaning: minimum value of f over C, equal to f(x*)

After \(T\ge1\) iterations, \[\min_{0\le k<T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\le \frac{R^2}{2\alpha T}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}\] for the raw policy. If every \(g_k\ne0\), then for the normalized policy, \[\min_{0\le k<T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\le \frac{GR^2}{2\ell T}+\frac{G\ell}{2}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-Norm Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of raw and normalized policies under variation in selected subgradient norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_k\ne0\) be a selected subgradient. Before any projection, the constant-stepsize update \(z_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha g_k\) satisfies
\[
\lVert z_{k+1}-x_k\rVert_2=\alpha\lVert g_k\rVert_2,
\]
whereas the constant-step-length update \(\widehat z_{k+1}=x_k-\ell g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2\) satisfies
\[
\lVert\widehat z_{k+1}-x_k\rVert_2=\ell.
\]
Consequently, scaling the chosen subgradient by a positive factor changes the raw-step displacement but leaves the normalized displacement unchanged. After Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set containing \(x_k\), each realized displacement is no larger than its corresponding pre-projection displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw-step motion scales with the subgradient norm, while normalized motion is invariant to positive rescaling; projection can only shorten either move.
assumptions_latex: If projection is used, \(C\) is closed and convex with \(x_k\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle-Selection Sensitivity at a Nonsmooth Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Different valid subgradient selections at one point produce different raw and normalized motions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\) at \(x=0\), \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\). A raw step selected with \(g\in[-1,1]\) has displacement \(\alpha|g|\in[0,\alpha]\). A normalized step has length \(\ell\) for every \(g\ne0\), whereas \(g=0\) invokes the stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the same nonsmooth point, oracle choice can make a raw step arbitrarily small, produce a full normalized step, or trigger stopping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A vanishing but summable schedule can exhaust its travel before reaching a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\), let \(A=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k<\infty\), and choose \(x_0>A\). Then \[x_k=x_0-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\alpha_j\longrightarrow x_0-A>0.\] Thus \(\alpha_k\to0\) alone does not ensure convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If total step length is finite, the method can start farther away than it can ever travel and converge nonoptimally.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Summable Diminishing Steps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of standard predetermined power-law stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha_k=a(k+1)^{-p}\), \(a>0\), \(p>0\), one has \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\iff p\le1\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\iff p>1/2\). Hence \(1/2<p\le1\) is the classical nonsummable, square-summable range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-law steps vanish for every positive exponent, are nonsummable through exponent one, and are square-summable above one half.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Law Diminishing Schedules

assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical diminishing-stepsize projected-subgradient convergence theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convergence theorem for predetermined diminishing projected-subgradient stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and define \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\). Suppose \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\|g_k\|\leq G\), and the predetermined stepsizes satisfy \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2<\infty\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\to0\) and \(\min_{0\leq j\leq k}f(x_j)\to f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For projected subgradient iterates with uniformly bounded subgradients and an attained minimum, positive stepsizes that vanish, are nonsummable, and are square-summable force the distance to the solution set and the best observed objective gap to converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Stepsize Families

children.title: Polyak Stepsize Family
children.top_down_role: Objective-level-informed policies and their target-estimation variants.

children.title: Known Optimal-Value Regime
children.top_down_role: The classical exact target-information regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-Iterate Bound for Exact-Target Polyak Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-iteration guarantee under bounded subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the relaxed Polyak iteration with constant \(\gamma\in(0,2)\), if \(\|g_k\|\le G\) for \(0\le k<T\), then for every \(x^*\in X^*\), \[\min_{0\le k<T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\le\frac{G\|x_0-x^*\|}{\sqrt{\gamma(2-\gamma)T}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded subgradients, the best relaxed exact-target Polyak iterate has an inverse-square-root gap bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Bound for Exact-Target Polyak Steps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure at and beyond the upper endpoint of the relaxed Polyak interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(f^*=0\), and \(x_0\ne0\), the relaxed Polyak step gives \(x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma)x_k\). Thus \(\gamma=2\) produces a two-cycle, while \(\gamma>2\) makes \(|x_k|=(\gamma-1)^k|x_0|\) diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper endpoint two is sharp: it causes cycling, and larger relaxation causes divergence on an absolute-value objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Relaxation Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental distance decrease for exact-target Polyak steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(f^*=\min_C f\) is known, and \(\alpha_k=\gamma(f(x_k)-f^*)/\|g_k\|^2\) with \(0<\gamma<2\). Then for every \(x^*\in X^*\), \[\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|^2\le\|x_k-x^*\|^2-\gamma(2-\gamma)\frac{(f(x_k)-f^*)^2}{\|g_k\|^2}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relaxed exact-target Polyak step with relaxation between zero and two decreases squared distance to every minimizer.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Polyak Fejer Decrease
Known Optimal-Value Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected Polyak steps with exact knowledge of the minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), a convex function \(f\), its known minimum value \(f^*\), and \(x_0\in C\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(f(x_k)=f^*\), stop and output \(x_k\). Otherwise set \(\alpha_k=(f(x_k)-f^*)/\|g_k\|^2\) and update \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\). After a prescribed number of oracle calls, output the best objective-value iterate encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical Polyak policy divides the current exact optimality gap by the squared subgradient norm before taking a projected step.

notation.meaning: subgradient selected at the current iterate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and exact-target Polyak update fit the terminal container, but no inspectable source citation is supplied.

children.title: Estimated Target-Level Regime
children.top_down_role: Target-level variants used without exact knowledge of the optimum value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failures demonstrating why an estimated target requires a specified update mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), \(f^*=0\), and \(\alpha_k=[f(x_k)-\ell]_+/|g_k|^2\): if \(\ell>0\), every \(x_0\) with \(0<|x_0|\le\ell\) has \(\alpha_0=0\) and stalls; if \(\ell=-\delta<0\), \(x_0=\delta\), and \(g_k=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\), then \(x_k=(-1)^k\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target above the optimum can stall prematurely, while a target below it can produce persistent oscillation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell>f^*\text{ may stall suboptimally, while }\ell<f^*\text{ may generate a nonconvergent cycle}
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Target-Misspecification Failures
Estimated Target-Level Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak-type steps driven by an estimated target level rather than the exact optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in C\), target estimates \((\ell_k)_{k\geq0}\), and relaxation factors \(\gamma_k\in(0,2)\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), stop and output \(x_k\). Otherwise set \(\alpha_k=\gamma_k[f(x_k)-\ell_k]_+/\|g_k\|^2\) and \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\). The level-update rule may lower, raise, or restart \(\ell_k\) using observed objective values; after \(T\) calls, output an iterate attaining \(\min_{0\leq j<T}f(x_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An estimated-level method replaces the unknown optimum in Polyak's formula by an adaptively maintained target and returns the best observed iterate.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: current estimate of the target objective level

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic algorithm template fits the estimated-target container and makes no convergence claim, but the admissible target-update behavior is too variant-dependent to certify without a specific source.

children.title: Horizon-Free Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Policies that avoid advance commitment to a stopping horizon.

children.title: Horizon-Free Schedules
children.top_down_role: Schedules usable without a predetermined stopping time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rates induced by power-law steps in the standard weighted-average subgradient bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\|x_0-x^*\|\le R\), \(\|g_k\|\le G\), and \(\alpha_k=a(k+1)^{-p}\) with \(a>0\) and \(0<p<1\), then the standard weighted-average bound yields \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*=O(T^{-p})\) for \(p<1/2\), \(O((\log T)/\sqrt T)\) for \(p=1/2\), and \(O(T^{-(1-p)})\) for \(p>1/2\). Moreover, \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), while \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\) exactly when \(p>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-law horizon-free schedules have three standard weighted-average rate regimes, with a logarithmic factor at inverse-square-root decay.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Horizon-Free Schedule Rates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when a schedule has finite cumulative travel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\), let \(S=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k<\infty\) with \(\alpha_k>0\), and start from \(x_0>S\). Choosing \(g_k=1\in\partial f(x_k)\) gives \(x_k\ge x_0-S>0\) for every \(k\), so the iterates do not approach the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule with finite total step length can fail even for the absolute-value objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable-Step Failure Boundary

notation.meaning: fixed positive scale parameter, commonly an initial-distance bound
fixed positive scale parameter, commonly a subgradient-norm bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: definition of a predetermined horizon-free stepsize schedule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and standard example of a predetermined schedule computable without a terminal horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A predetermined stepsize schedule \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) is horizon-free if, for every \(k\geq0\), the value \(\alpha_k\) is determined by \(k\) and fixed problem parameters and does not depend on a terminal horizon \(T\). For example, for fixed \(R>0\) and \(G>0\), the schedule \(\alpha_k=R/(G\sqrt{k+1})\) is horizon-free, positive, vanishing, and nonsummable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predetermined schedule is horizon-free when every stepsize can be computed from the iteration index and fixed parameters without knowing when the run will terminate; inverse-square-root steps are a standard example.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Free Schedules

children.title: Unknown-Horizon Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Policy selection when the eventual run length is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational characterization of a policy executable without knowing its stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic policy is unknown-horizon admissible if \(\alpha_k=\Phi_k(H_k)\), where \(H_k\) contains only information revealed through iteration \(k\). Equivalently, runs having the same history through \(k\) but different terminal horizons \(T,T'>k\) choose the same \(\alpha_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown-horizon admissibility is nonanticipation, equivalently prefix consistency across future stopping times.
assumptions_latex: H_k\text{ contains only information available through iteration }k

notation.meaning: history available when step k is selected

knowledge_statements.title: Prefix-Consistent Unknown-Horizon Policy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon-Tuned Policies Are Not Prefix Consistent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between open-ended policies and rules requiring an announced horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rule \(\alpha_k^{(T)}=R/(G\sqrt T)\) for \(0\le k<T\) is horizon tuned: if \(T\ne T'\), then \(\alpha_0^{(T)}\ne\alpha_0^{(T')}\). It therefore requires replacement by a horizon-free schedule or conversion through an adaptation mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step chosen from the final run length is not one unknown-horizon policy because its initial action changes with the future horizon.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Tuned Policies Are Not Prefix Consistent

assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: stepsize-weighted average of the first T iterates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon validity of the projected-subgradient averaging bound when stepsizes are selected online.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and define \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\). Suppose \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\|g_k\|\leq G\), and each \(\alpha_k>0\) is chosen from information available through iteration \(k\), without using a terminal horizon. For \(T\geq1\), define \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k)\). Then, for every \(x^*\in X^*\) and every integer \(T\geq1\), \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\leq(\|x_0-x^*\|^2+G^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2)/(2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex projected subgradient iterations whose positive stepsizes are chosen online, the usual weighted-average objective bound holds at every deterministic evaluation horizon, so no terminal iteration must be fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Horizon Adaptation

children.title: Doubling-Trick Policies
children.top_down_role: Epoch-based conversion of horizon-tuned policies to open-ended operation.

knowledge_statements.title: Doubling-Trick Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epoch restarts convert known-horizon steps into an unknown-horizon policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume known bounds \(R\geq\|x-x^*\|\) for admissible epoch starts and \(G\geq\|g\|\). Partition time into epochs \(E_j\) of lengths \(H_j=2^j\). At epoch \(j\), restart the projected subgradient method from the preceding epoch output, use the constant step \(\alpha_j=R/(G\sqrt{H_j})\), and form the average of that epoch's iterates. At any interruption, output the average from the most recently completed epoch, or the current epoch average if none is complete. The policy never uses the eventual stopping horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The doubling trick runs successively doubled, horizon-tuned epochs and returns a completed epoch average, producing an online policy without knowing the final horizon.

notation.meaning: constant stepsize used within epoch j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic kind fits the leaf, but the restart, averaging, and interruption-output conventions are variant-specific and have no inspectable citation. The stated radius condition also requires source-level confirmation for the claimed epoch construction.

children.title: Anytime Output Certification
children.top_down_role: Quality reporting at unscheduled interruption times.

assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: computable upper certificate for the objective gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A computable upper bound accompanying each weighted-average projected-subgradient output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and define \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\). Suppose \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\alpha_k>0\), and \(\|g_k\|\leq G\). If a known \(R\) satisfies \(\|x_0-x^*\|\leq R\) for some \(x^*\in X^*\), then at each integer \(T\geq1\) one may output \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k)\) together with \(U_T=(R^2+G^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2)/(2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k)\). These quantities satisfy \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\leq U_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex projected subgradient iterations with known initial-distance and subgradient bounds, every weighted-average output has a computable upper certificate obtained from the recorded stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Output Certification

children.title: Classical Deterministic Extensions
children.top_down_role: Classical extensions using memory, decomposition, or changes of metric while retaining subgradient information.

children.title: Multistep Subgradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods combining information from multiple past oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Multistep Subgradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic Euclidean scheme aggregating several stored subgradient responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a memory length \(m\geq1\), choose \(x_0\in C\), and query \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). At iteration \(k\), select coefficients \(\beta_{k,j}\) for \(j=\max\{0,k-m+1\},\ldots,k\), form \(d_k=\sum_j\beta_{k,j}g_j\), choose \(\alpha_k>0\), and update \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_kd_k)\). A stopping rule may use a fixed oracle budget or a stationarity test; the finite-budget output is the best objective-value iterate. Particular multistep methods specify the coefficient rule and conditions ensuring descent or convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistep method forms its search direction from a weighted combination of several recent subgradients before projecting the new iterate.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: aggregation coefficient for stored subgradient j

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Multistep Methods p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Multistep Methods p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed Aggregation Need Not Preserve Subgradient Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for unrestricted multistep coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\) at \(x=0\), both \(g_1=1\) and \(g_2=-1\) belong to \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\). Signed coefficients \(\beta_1=2\), \(\beta_2=-1\), despite summing to one, give \(d=2g_1-g_2=3\notin\partial f(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed affine aggregation of valid subgradients can produce a vector that is not a subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed Aggregation Need Not Preserve Subgradient Validity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a convex combination of stale subgradients as an inexact subgradient at the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\beta_{k,j}\geq0\), \(\sum_j\beta_{k,j}=1\), \(g_j\in\partial f(x_j)\), and \(d_k:=\sum_j\beta_{k,j}g_j\). Define \[\varepsilon_k:=\sum_j\beta_{k,j}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x_j)-\langle g_j,x_k-x_j\rangle\bigr)\geq0.\] Then \(d_k\in\partial_{\varepsilon_k}f(x_k)\), that is, \[f(y)\geq f(x_k)+\langle d_k,y-x_k\rangle-\varepsilon_k\qquad\text{for every }y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex combination of stored exact subgradients is an epsilon-subgradient at the current iterate, with an explicit staleness error.
knowledge_statements.title: Stored-Subgradient Epsilon-Subgradient Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of multistep directions analyzed as epsilon-subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_kd_k)\), where \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(f\) is convex and Lipschitz on \(C\), \(X^*\neq\varnothing\), \(d_k\in\partial_{\varepsilon_k}f(x_k)\), and \(\|d_k\|\leq G\). If \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\to0\) and \(f(x_k)\to f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistep method converges when its aggregate directions are bounded epsilon-subgradients and the stepsize-weighted staleness errors are summable.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex
\(f\) is convex and Lipschitz on \(C\), with \(X^*\neq\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence Through Summable Aggregation Error

children.title: Incremental Subgradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Deterministic componentwise methods for finite-sum and decomposable objectives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic incremental variant that projects only after a complete component sweep.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex, and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Set \(z_{k,0}=x_k\); for a prescribed component order choose \(g_{k,i}\in\partial f_i(z_{k,i-1})\) and set \(z_{k,i}=z_{k,i-1}-\alpha_kg_{k,i}\). Complete the cycle with \[x_{k+1}=P_C(z_{k,m})=P_C\!\left(x_k-\alpha_k\sum_{i=1}^mg_{k,i}\right).\] A fixed cyclic order or a prescribed permutation per cycle is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic incremental sweep may take all component steps in the ambient space and project once after the cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex for every \(i\)
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex

notation.meaning: unprojected inner iterate after component i

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Projection Incremental Cycle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-component-subgradient estimate for the projected-after-each-component cyclic method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the projected-after-each-component cyclic method in the deferred seed, suppose \(\|g_{k,i}\|\leq L_i\) and let \(L:=\sum_{i=1}^mL_i\). Then every \(y\in C\) satisfies \[\|x_{k+1}-y\|^2\leq\|x_k-y\|^2-2\alpha_k\bigl(f(x_k)-f(y)\bigr)+\alpha_k^2L^2.\] Consequently, if \(x^*\in X^*\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k>0\), then \[\min_{0\leq k<K}(f(x_k)-f^*)\leq\frac{\|x_0-x^*\|^2+L^2\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k^2}{2\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One complete projected incremental cycle satisfies the standard subgradient potential inequality with the sum of component norm bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex at all encountered inner points
Every component is processed exactly once per cycle
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental-Cycle Fundamental Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diminishing-Stepsize Convergence of Cyclic Incremental Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic convergence for the projected-after-each-component cyclic method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X^*\neq\varnothing\), the component subgradient bounds of the incremental-cycle inequality hold, and \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k=\infty\), \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k^2<\infty\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\to0\) and \(f(x_k)\to f^*\). In particular, if \(X^*=\{x^*\}\), then \(x_k\to x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded component subgradients and square-summable but nonsummable steps, cyclic incremental subgradient iterates approach the solution set and their values approach the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\|g_{k,i}\|\leq L_i\) at all encountered inner points
knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing-Stepsize Convergence of Cyclic Incremental Subgradients
Incremental Subgradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic componentwise projected subgradient updates for convex finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), with each \(f_i\) convex. Given \(x_k\in C\), set \(z_{k,0}=x_k\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), select \(g_{k,i}\in\partial f_i(z_{k,i-1})\) and set \(z_{k,i}=P_C(z_{k,i-1}-\alpha_k g_{k,i})\). Complete the cycle with \(x_{k+1}=z_{k,m}\). Stop after a prescribed number of component-oracle calls or cycles, and output the best recorded outer iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclic incremental method processes one convex component at a time, projecting after every component subgradient step and defining one outer iterate per cycle.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

notation.meaning: inner iterate after component i in cycle k
subgradient of component i at its inner iterate

children.title: Optimal Subgradient-Type Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical optimal-method constructions associated with nonsmooth oracle complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Subgradient-Type Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax first-order oracle complexity for Lipschitz convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing a convex \(G\)-Lipschitz function over a Euclidean ball containing an optimizer within distance \(R\) of the initial query. In the black-box first-order oracle model and dimensions large enough for the lower-bound construction, the minimax number of oracle calls needed to guarantee \(f(\hat x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\) is \(\Theta(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\). Projected subgradient-type methods with appropriately tuned steps and averaging attain the upper order, while a resisting-oracle family supplies the matching lower order; constants depend on the precise oracle and domain conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For general Lipschitz convex objectives, optimal first-order methods require and suffice with order squared inverse accuracy oracle calls.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical nonsmooth convex oracle-complexity rate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind is appropriate for the stated minimax claim, but the matching upper and lower bounds depend on precise domain, oracle, dimension, and output conventions. No source locator is supplied to certify those conventions.

children.title: Shor's r-Algorithm

knowledge_statements.title: Shor's r-Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one space dilation driven by changes in normalized transformed subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a nonsingular matrix \(B_0\), and a dilation factor \(r>1\). At iteration \(k\), query \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), form \(p_k=B_k^{\mathsf T}g_k/\|B_k^{\mathsf T}g_k\|\), and take \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h_kB_kp_k\). When \(k\geq1\) and \(u_k=p_k-p_{k-1}\neq0\), apply the rank-one dilation \(B_{k+1}=B_k(I+(r-1)u_ku_k^{\mathsf T}/\|u_k\|^2)\); otherwise retain \(B_{k+1}=B_k\). Stop by a prescribed budget or subgradient-based test and return the best observed iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shor's space-dilation family takes transformed normalized subgradient steps and updates the transformation by a rank-one dilation based on successive directions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Shor's named r-algorithm leaf, but the normalization, rank-one update, multiplication order, and dilation parameter conventions are historically variant-sensitive. The supplied standard-field rationale is insufficient to certify this exact formula.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extracted recurrence for Shor's space-dilation subgradient algorithm. The step-size indexing follows the source: choose t_{k+1} for a future iteration while the current update uses t_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\), \(B_1=I\), and \(t_1>0\). Select \(\xi_0\in\partial f(x_0)\), and set \(x_1=x_0-t_1\xi_0\), \(\bar\xi_1=\xi_0\), and \(k=1\). While the termination condition is not met, select \(\xi_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), set \(\xi_k^*=B_k^T\xi_k\) and \(r_k=\xi_k^*-\bar\xi_k\), and, when \(r_k\ne0\), define \(s_k=r_k/\lVert r_k\rVert\). Form \(R_\beta(s_k)=I+(\beta-1)s_ks_k^T\), update \(B_{k+1}=B_kR_\beta(s_k)\), and set \(\bar\xi_{k+1}=B_{k+1}^T\xi_k\). Choose \(t_{k+1}\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k-t_kB_{k+1}\bar\xi_{k+1}\), and increment \(k\). Upon termination, return \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a point, a dilation parameter between zero and one, the identity transformation, and a positive initial step size. After an initial subgradient step, repeatedly transform a selected subgradient, normalize its difference from the stored transformed subgradient when that difference is nonzero, apply the resulting rank-one space dilation, and update the iterate. The source chooses the next step size before performing the current update with the previously indexed step size. Return the final iterate upon termination.
assumptions_latex: \xi_k\in\partial f(x_k)\text{ is selectable at each generated iterate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure generates space-dilated subgradient iterates and returns the final iterate }x_k\text{ upon termination.}

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Subgradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient steps in a changing positive-definite quadratic metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Given \(x_0\in C\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H_k\), and \(\alpha_k>0\), then set \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\langle g_k,x-x_k\rangle+(2\alpha_k)^{-1}\|x-x_k\|_{H_k}^2\}\). Uniform metric control requires constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\) with \(mI\preceq H_k\preceq MI\). Stop under a stated oracle budget or stationarity test and return the best iterate or a weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-metric subgradient method replaces Euclidean projection by a proximal subproblem whose positive-definite quadratic metric may change at every iteration.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

children.title: Euclidean Norm Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) is equipped with the inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}y\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean norm and its dual norm.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Euclidean self-duality and the quadratic Bregman identity are standard finite-dimensional convex-analysis facts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean geometry with the standard quadratic reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\|x\|_2=(x^{\mathsf T}x)^{1/2}\) and \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\). Under the canonical identification of \(E\) with its dual, the dual norm satisfies \(\|z\|_{2,*}=\sup_{\|x\|_2\leq1}\langle z,x\rangle=\|z\|_2\). Moreover, \(\nabla h(y)=y\), so the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2.\] Thus quadratic reference geometry recovers the self-dual Euclidean norm pair and squared Euclidean displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean norm is self-dual, and the Bregman divergence of one-half the squared Euclidean norm is one-half the squared Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Norm Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically precise and fits the Euclidean-geometry leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Euclidean space is a finite-dimensional vector space \(\mathbb{E}\) endowed with an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). Its Euclidean norm is the induced norm \(\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{E}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean space is a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with an inner product. The Euclidean norm of a vector is the square root of its inner product with itself.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Column-Rank Pullback Euclidean Norm and Its Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the Euclidean norm pulled back through an injective linear map and the corresponding inverse-metric dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} have full column rank, let \|\cdot\|_{\mathbb{R}^m} be the Euclidean norm, and set G=A^TA. Define \|x\|_{\mathbb{R}^n}:=\|Ax\|_{\mathbb{R}^m}^*. Since the Euclidean norm is self-dual, G\succ0 and, for every x,g\in\mathbb{R}^n, \[\|x\|_{\mathbb{R}^n}=\sqrt{\langle Gx,x\rangle}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\langle a_i,x\rangle^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad \|g\|_{\mathbb{R}^n}^*=\sqrt{\langle g,G^{-1}g\rangle},\] where a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n are the columns of A^T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-column-rank matrix pulls the Euclidean norm back to a Euclidean norm on its domain. The induced metric is G=AᵀA, and the dual norm is determined by the inverse metric G⁻¹.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\text{ has full column rank}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Quadratic Minimization of a Linear Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded closed form for minimizing a linear functional plus the Euclidean quadratic reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb E_1=\mathbb R^n\) have the Euclidean norm, let \(\mathbb E_2=\mathbb R^m\) have the standard inner product, and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). For every \(\hat u\in\mathbb E_2\), the problem
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb E_1}\left\{\langle Ax,\hat u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}+\frac12\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}^2\right\}
\]
has the unique minimizer
\[
x_0(\hat u)=-A^T\hat u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Euclidean geometry, a linear functional plus one half of the squared norm has a unique minimizer equal to the negative adjoint image of the linear-functional coefficient.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1=\mathbb R^n\text{ with the Euclidean norm}
\mathbb E_2=\mathbb R^m\text{ with the standard inner product}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb E_1}\left\{\langle Ax,\hat u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}+\frac12\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}^2\right\}=\{-A^T\hat u\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Representation and Gradient of a Euclidean Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded value-function representation and differentiability formula obtained by minimizing weighted affine models plus a Euclidean quadratic reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb E_1\) and \(\mathbb E_2=\mathbb R^m\) be Euclidean spaces with their induced norms. Given \(g_j,x_j\in\mathbb E_1\) and \(f_j\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
b^{(j)}=\langle g_j,x_j\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}-f_j,
\qquad A^Tu=\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}g_j,
\qquad (Ax)^{(j)}=\langle g_j,x\rangle_{\mathbb E_1},
\]
and
\[
\phi(u)=\min_{x\in\mathbb E_1}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\bigl[f_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}\bigr]+\frac12\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}^2\right\}.
\]
Then, for every \(u\in\mathbb R^m\),
\[
\phi(u)=-\langle b,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\frac12\|A^Tu\|_{\mathbb E_1}^{*2}.
\]
Moreover, \(\phi\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^m\) and
\[
\nabla\phi(u)=-b-AA^Tu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the weighted affine models plus one half of the squared Euclidean norm yields a concave quadratic value function. Its value is the negative linear term in b minus one half of the squared dual norm of the adjoint image, and its gradient is minus b minus A times that image.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1\text{ and }\mathbb E_2=\mathbb R^m\text{ are Euclidean spaces with induced norms}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vector and matrix norm pairs used in adapted geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conjugate exponents \(1\le p,q\le\infty\), \(1/p+1/q=1\), the dual of \(\|\cdot\|_p\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) is \(\|\cdot\|_q\). The dual of the Schatten \(p\)-norm is the Schatten \(q\)-norm. In particular, these include the \(\ell_1/\ell_\infty\) and nuclear/operator pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugate-exponent lp and Schatten norms form the standard vector and matrix non-Euclidean dual families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm geometries chosen to reflect domain or oracle structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A non-Euclidean geometry is specified by a primal norm \(\|\cdot\|\) and its dual \(\|z\|_* = \sup_{\|x\|\leq1}\langle z,x\rangle\). Typical pairs include \((\|\cdot\|_1,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\) for simplex or sparse-coordinate structure and \((\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{tr}},\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}})\) for matrices. The domain is measured in the primal norm, whereas subgradients and oracle errors are measured in the dual norm. Unlike Euclidean geometry, the primal and dual norms generally differ, and a compatible strongly convex distance generator supplies the corresponding prox geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-Euclidean mirror geometry pairs a domain-adapted primal norm with its dual, such as l1/linfinity or trace/operator norms.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Euclidean Norm Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Induced norm and bounds for a signed stacking operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator from a normed primal space to \(\mathbb R^{2m}\) equipped with the \(\ell_1\)-norm; the source's max-based definitions presuppose attainment of the displayed maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathbb E_1,\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_1})\) be a normed space, with dual norm \(\|a\|_1^*:=\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}|\langle a,x\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}|\). Let \(A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb R^m\) have rows \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb E_1^*\), and set \(\hat A=(A;-A):\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb R^{2m}\). Equip \(\mathbb R^{2m}\) with \(\|u\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^{2m}|u^{(j)}|\), and define \(\|\hat A\|_{1,2}:=\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}\|\hat A x\|_1\). Assuming the displayed maxima are attained, \[\|\hat A\|_{1,2}=2\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}\sum_{j=1}^m|\langle a_j,x\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}|,\] and consequently \[2\max_{1\le j\le m}\|a_j\|_1^*\le \|\hat A\|_{1,2}\le 2\sum_{j=1}^m\|a_j\|_1^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the max-based norm definitions are well-defined, stacking A and negative A and using the l1 norm on the range makes the induced norm twice the maximum sum of absolute row evaluations on the primal unit sphere. It lies between twice the largest row dual norm and twice the sum of all row dual norms.
assumptions_latex: (\mathbb E_1,\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_1})\text{ is a normed space}
\text{the maxima used in the displayed norm definitions are attained}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper bound for a weighted induced operator norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the induced bilinear norm under a problem-adapted weighted Euclidean geometry. To make the displayed weighted expression a genuine norm, every row functional must be nonzero; otherwise it is only a seminorm and zero rows must be removed or quotiented out.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathbb E_1$ be a finite-dimensional normed vector space, let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb E_1^*$ satisfy $\|a_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*>0$ for every $j$, and define $A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb R^m$ by $(Ax)^{(j)}=\langle a_j,x\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}$. Equip $\mathbb E_2=\mathbb R^m$ with
\[
\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^m\|a_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*(u^{(j)})^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Then
\[
\|A\|_{1,2}:=\max_{\substack{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}\le1\\\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}\le1}}
\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\langle a_j,x\rangle_{\mathbb E_1}
\le\left(\sum_{j=1}^m\|a_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*\right)^{1/2}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the componentwise linear map determined by nonzero functionals a_j and the stated weighted Euclidean codomain norm, the induced bilinear operator norm is at most the square root of the sum of their dual norms.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1\text{ is a finite-dimensional normed vector space}

children.top_down_role: Domain distances, radii, plus prox curvature measured in the primal norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurement of distance-generator curvature in the selected primal norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A differentiable convex generator \(h\) has primal-norm strong-convexity modulus \(\sigma>0\) on \(Q\) when \[D_h(x,y)\ge\frac{\sigma}{2}\|x-y\|^2\qquad(x,y\in Q).\] The largest valid modulus measures prox curvature in the same primal units as domain displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox curvature is the strong-convexity modulus comparing Bregman divergence with squared primal-norm displacement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Center-optimized radius of a bounded domain in the selected primal norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(Q\subset E\), define \[\operatorname{rad}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q):=\inf_{c\in E}\sup_{x\in Q}\|x-c\|.\] Then \[\tfrac12\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q)\le\operatorname{rad}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q)\le\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q).\] In finite dimensions, nonempty compact \(Q\) admits a minimizing center.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest centered primal-norm radius lies between one-half and one times the domain diameter, and compact domains have a center.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurement of feasible-domain displacement in the selected primal norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty feasible set \(Q\subseteq E\), its primal-norm diameter is \[\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q):=\sup\{\|x-y\|:x,y\in Q\}.\] A radius about a specified center \(x_0\in E\) is analogously \(R_{\|\cdot\|}(Q;x_0):=\sup_{x\in Q}\|x-x_0\|\). The diameter is finite if and only if \(Q\) is bounded in \(\|\cdot\|\), and it satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q)\leq2R_{\|\cdot\|}(Q;x_0)\) whenever the radius is finite. These quantities measure domain displacement in the primal geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-norm diameter is the supremum of distances between feasible points; a centered radius measures distance from a chosen reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform measurement of subgradient-oracle outputs in the norm dual to domain geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a primal norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(E\), define its dual norm on \(E^*\) by \(\|g\|_*:=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}\langle g,u\rangle\). For a feasible set \(Q\) and oracle-output correspondence \(G:Q\rightrightarrows E^*\), the uniform oracle magnitude is \[M_*:=\sup_{x\in Q}\sup_{g\in G(x)}\|g\|_*.\] If an oracle selects one output \(g(x)\in G(x)\), its realized magnitude is \(\|g(x)\|_*\). Measuring oracle outputs in the dual norm makes their pairing with primal displacements compatible with norm duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle size is measured by the dual norm, usually through a uniform bound on all subgradients returned over the feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Norm Oracle Measurement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual-norm oracle bound is well-defined and appropriate for this leaf, but it has no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Norm-Duality Pairing
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between domain geometry, oracle scale, plus associated complexity parameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment certificate for primal-dual norm equality in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonzero \(x\in E\), there exists \(g_x\in E^*\) such that \(\|g_x\|_*=1\) and \(\langle g_x,x\rangle=\|x\|\). Conversely, any such functional certifies the primal norm and equality in generalized Hölder.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit dual norming functional attains the primal norm and certifies equality in the pairing bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Norming Functional Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy between squared primal and dual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), \[\phi^*(g)=\tfrac12\|g\|_*^2.\] Equivalently, \(\langle g,x\rangle\le\tfrac12\|x\|^2+\tfrac12\|g\|_*^2\), with equality exactly when \(g\in\partial\phi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the squared primal norm and half the squared dual norm are Fenchel conjugates, yielding the norm-pair Young inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Squared-Norm Fenchel Duality

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional with norm \(\|\cdot\|\), dual space \(E^*\), and canonical pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Associated dual norm on the dual space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The support-function definition of a dual norm and generalized Hölder inequality are standard.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical pairing between primal displacements and dual oracle vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The norm dual to \(\|\cdot\|\) is the support function of its closed unit ball: \[\|g\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}\langle g,x\rangle.\] Consequently, every \(x\in E\) and \(g\in E^*\) satisfy the generalized Hölder inequality \[|\langle g,x\rangle|\leq\|g\|_*\|x\|.\] In finite dimensions the converse support representation also holds, \(\|x\|=\sup_{\|g\|_*\leq1}\langle g,x\rangle\). Thus primal displacement and dual oracle magnitude form a mutually determining norm pair under the canonical bilinear pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm and its dual are mutual support functions, and their pairing is bounded by the product of primal and dual magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Duality Pairing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual norm, generalized Hölder inequality, and finite-dimensional bidual representation are correct and the duality content kind fits, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Quadratic Distance Generators
children.top_down_role: Reference functions yielding Euclidean and preconditioned quadratic geometries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of norm geometry when the quadratic matrix is singular or indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(H\succeq0\) is singular, then \(D_h(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}H(x-y)\) vanishes whenever \(x-y\in\ker H\), so it defines only a seminorm geometry. If \(H\) has a negative eigenvalue, \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular positive-semidefinite quadratic loses separation along its kernel, while an indefinite quadratic is not a convex distance generator.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Quadratic Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Invariance of Quadratic Bregman Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic generators inducing the same divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+a^{\mathsf T}x+c\), with \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), \[D_h(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}H(x-y).\] Thus affine additions do not alter the Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only the quadratic Hessian determines a quadratic Bregman divergence; affine terms cancel.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance of Quadratic Bregman Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic generators, including Euclidean and preconditioned cases.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 The proximal gradient method for convex programs p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be symmetric positive definite and define \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Since \(\nabla h(y)=Hy\), its Bregman divergence has the representation \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle Hy,x-y\rangle=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}H(x-y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_H^2.\] The generator is strongly convex with modulus \(1\) relative to \(\|\cdot\|_H\). Taking \(H=I\) yields ordinary Euclidean geometry; a general \(H\) yields a linearly preconditioned quadratic geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic generates one-half the squared distance in its induced norm; the identity matrix recovers Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Distance Generators

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 The proximal gradient method for convex programs p. 93

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic Bregman representation is correct and fits the generator leaf, but the cited proximal-gradient section does not clearly support the general positive-definite Bregman identity and relative strong-convexity claim without full-text inspection.

children.title: Entropy Distance Generators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel representation of simplex-restricted negative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i+\delta_{\Delta_n}(x)\), \[h^*(s)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{s_i}\right),\qquad (\nabla h^*(s))_i=\frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex negative entropy is Fenchel-dual to log-sum-exp, whose gradient is softmax.
knowledge_statements.title: Entropy–Log-Sum-Exp Conjugacy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value boundary behavior of entropy divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(0\log(0/y_i)=0\) and \(x_i\log(x_i/0)=+\infty\) for \(x_i>0\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)<\infty\) only if \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(y)\). The classical entropy gradient is unavailable when a reference coordinate \(y_i\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is infinite under support mismatch, and its Bregman formula requires a positive reference on the support of the first argument.

notation.meaning: Indices at which x is positive.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy Support Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unnormalized entropy geometry on positive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\sum_i(x_i\log x_i-x_i)\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_i\left(x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}-x_i+y_i\right).\] On an equal-mass slice, the linear terms cancel and the expression reduces to \(\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unnormalized negative entropy generates generalized relative entropy and reduces to KL divergence on equal-mass slices.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Orthant Entropy Divergence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Negative entropy and its Kullback-Leibler Bregman divergence are standard simplex geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-entropy geometry on the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the probability simplex \(\Delta_n\), define negative entropy by \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\), using \(0\log0=0\). For \(y\in\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\), the gradient has coordinates \((\nabla h(y))_i=1+\log y_i\), and the Bregman divergence is \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y),\qquad x\in\Delta_n.\] This generator is strictly convex and is strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|_1\) under the usual simplex normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy generates Kullback-Leibler divergence on the simplex and supplies geometry adapted to probability vectors and positive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Distance Generators

children.title: Barrier Distance Generators
children.top_down_role: Reference functions adapted to interiors of constrained convex domains or cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature conditions for a polyhedral logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\), \[v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2h(x)v=\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{(a_i^{\mathsf T}v)^2}{(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)^2}.\] Thus \(h\) is strictly convex exactly when \(\operatorname{span}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}=\mathbb R^n\). On a working subset where \(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le M_i<\infty\), it is \(\mu\)-strongly convex in Euclidean norm for \[\mu=\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\sum_i a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}/M_i^2\right)>0.\] Without spanning and upper slack control, a positive global Euclidean modulus need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity requires spanning constraint normals, while uniform Euclidean strong convexity also requires upper control of the slacks.
assumptions_latex: For the uniform modulus, \(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le M_i\) on the working subset.

notation.meaning: Euclidean strong-convexity modulus on the restricted set

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity and Strong-Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Scope of Log-Barrier Boundary Blow-Up
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correction of boundary blow-up for unbounded polyhedral domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_k\) converges to a finite boundary point \(\bar x\) of the closed polyhedron while \(x_k\) remains strictly feasible, then \(h(x_k)\to+\infty\), because at least one slack tends to zero and every slack remains bounded above. More generally, blow-up follows whenever some slack tends to zero and all slacks remain uniformly bounded above. On an unbounded domain, the vanishing of one slack alone is insufficient: for \(Q=\mathbb R_{++}^2\), \(h(x)=-\log x_1-\log x_2\), and \(x_k=(1/k,k)\), one slack tends to zero but \(h(x_k)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log barrier blows up at finite boundary approaches, but a vanishing slack alone does not force blow-up along an unbounded sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x)=-\sum_i\log(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\) on a nonempty strict-feasibility domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to\bar x\in\partial Q\Rightarrow h(x_k)\to+\infty\); this implication can fail when \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Scope of Log-Barrier Boundary Blow-Up

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-Concordance of the Polyhedral Logarithmic Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic third-order curvature of the standard logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\) and every direction \(v\), \[|D^3h(x)[v,v,v]|\le2\bigl(D^2h(x)[v,v]\bigr)^{3/2}.\] When the constraint normals span \(\mathbb R^n\), the Hessian local norm is nondegenerate and \(\|\nabla h(x)\|_{x,*}\le\sqrt m\); hence the standard polyhedral logarithmic barrier has barrier parameter at most \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard polyhedral logarithmic barrier is self-concordant and has barrier parameter at most the number of inequalities.
assumptions_latex: For the nondegenerate local dual norm, \(\operatorname{span}\{a_i\}=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Self-Concordance of the Polyhedral Logarithmic Barrier

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(x)=-\sum_i\log(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\) is convex on \(Q\) and diverges at every active-barrier boundary approach.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The logarithmic barrier and its Hessian are standard interior-point constructions.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic distance generation on the interior of a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the strictly feasible region \(Q=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x<b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), define \(s_i(x)=b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x\) and \[h(x):=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log s_i(x).\] Then \(h\) is smooth and convex on \(Q\), with \(\nabla^2h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}/s_i(x)^2\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\frac{s_i(x)}{s_i(y)}-1-\log\frac{s_i(x)}{s_i(y)}\right).\] Moreover, \(h(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever an active slack tends to zero along \(x_k\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logarithmic barrier generates an interior Bregman geometry whose curvature and value grow as constraint slacks approach zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Distance Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic-barrier Hessian, Bregman formula, and boundary behavior are internally consistent and fit the representation leaf, but no authoritative source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Curvature Lifts to Frobenius Matrix Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convexity and smoothness inherited by a trace-spectral generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. If \(t\mapsto\phi(t)-\tfrac\mu2t^2\) is convex on \(I\), then \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}\phi(X)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb S_I^n\) relative to Frobenius norm: \[D_h(X,Y)\ge\frac\mu2\|X-Y\|_F^2.\] If, additionally, \(\phi'\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(I\), then \[D_h(X,Y)\le\frac L2\|X-Y\|_F^2.\] Neither bound requires \(X\) and \(Y\) to commute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar strong convexity and smoothness lift to dimension-free Frobenius bounds for trace-spectral Bregman divergence.
assumptions_latex: For the upper bound, \(\phi'\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Curvature Lifts to Frobenius Matrix Curvature

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:I\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and convex on an interval \(I\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric matrices with spectrum in I.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Trace lifts of differentiable convex scalar functions are standard spectral convex functions.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-spectral generators on symmetric matrices with spectra in a fixed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and convex, and define the trace-spectral function \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}\phi(X)\) on \(\mathbb{S}_I^n\). Functional calculus gives \(\nabla h(Y)=\phi'(Y)\) under the trace pairing \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\). Hence \[D_h(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\phi(X)-\phi(Y)-\phi'(Y)(X-Y)\bigr)\geq0.\] When \(X\) and \(Y\) commute, this divergence reduces in their common eigenbasis to the sum of the scalar Bregman divergences of their paired eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex scalar function lifts through eigenvalue functional calculus to a trace-spectral generator with a matrix Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Distance Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trace-spectral construction and divergence formula fit the leaf, but the matrix derivative, convexity, and nonnegativity claims require a specific authoritative source locator.

children.title: Conic Matrix Generators
children.top_down_role: Distance-generating structures specialized to matrix cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form unconstrained cone-interior prox update and exact existence boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(G\in\mathbb S^n\), and \(\eta>0\), and put \(A=Y^{-1}+\eta G\). The problem \[\min_{X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n}\{\eta\langle G,X\rangle+D_h(X,Y)\}\] has a unique minimizer if and only if \(A\succ0\), in which case \[X^+=A^{-1}=(Y^{-1}+\eta G)^{-1}.\] If \(A\) has a nonpositive eigenvalue, the objective is unbounded below along a corresponding cone direction; thus positive semidefiniteness without definiteness is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-determinant mirror step updates the inverse matrix affinely exactly when the updated inverse is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Affine Log-Determinant Mirror Step

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Invariant Local Metric of the Log-Determinant Generator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian metric and congruence invariance on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(X)=-\log\det X\), \[\nabla^2h(X)[H]=X^{-1}HX^{-1},\qquad \langle H,\nabla^2h(X)[H]\rangle=\|X^{-1/2}HX^{-1/2}\|_F^2.\] Moreover, for every invertible \(A\), \[D_h(AXA^{\mathsf T},AYA^{\mathsf T})=D_h(X,Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-determinant Hessian defines an affine-invariant cone metric, and its divergence is congruence invariant.

notation.meaning: log-determinant Hessian local norm at X

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Invariant Local Metric of the Log-Determinant Generator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic barrier curvature on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(X)=-\log\det X\), every \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), and every symmetric direction \(H\), \[|D^3h(X)[H,H,H]|\le2\bigl(D^2h(X)[H,H]\bigr)^{3/2}.\] In the Hessian local dual norm, \(\|\nabla h(X)\|_{X,*}=\sqrt n\); hence \(-\log\det\) is an \(n\)-self-concordant barrier for the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log determinant is the canonical n-self-concordant barrier on the positive-definite cone.

notation.meaning: dual norm induced by the log-determinant Hessian

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Concordance of the Log-Determinant Barrier

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) is the interior of the positive-semidefinite cone, equipped with the trace pairing.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The log-determinant barrier and Stein-type divergence are standard positive-definite cone geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-determinant geometry on the positive-definite matrix cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), let \(h(X)=-\log\det X\). Under the trace pairing, \(\nabla h(Y)=-Y^{-1}\), and its Bregman divergence is \[D_h(X,Y)=-\log\det X+\log\det Y+\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Y^{-1}(X-Y)\bigr)\] \[=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{-1}X)-\log\det(Y^{-1}X)-n\geq0.\] The value tends to \(+\infty\) when \(X\) approaches a singular matrix from within \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\). Thus the log-determinant generator supplies an interior geometry adapted to the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative log determinant generates a nonnegative matrix divergence and becomes infinite as a positive-definite matrix approaches singularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Matrix Generators

assumptions_latex: \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) is considered on the closed simplex \(\Delta_n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary failure of differentiable entropic Bregman geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For negative entropy \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on \(\Delta_n\), the coordinate derivative \(1+\log x_i\) tends to \(-\infty\) as \(x_i\downarrow0\). Therefore \(h\) is finite on the closed simplex but is not differentiable at its boundary, so the gradient-based formula for \(D_h(x,y)\) requires \(y\in\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\). Its lower-semicontinuous extension satisfies \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(y).\] Hence a mirror step centered at a boundary point can be undefined or can exclude coordinates outside the center's support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropy remains finite at the simplex boundary, but its gradient fails there; finite relative entropy also requires support containment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Convexity Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for a noncompact Bregman proximal subproblem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite constrained prox mapping for a differentiable strongly convex reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\). For center \(y\in Q\), dual vector \(g\in E^*\), stepsize \(\eta>0\), and convex term \(\psi\), the Bregman proximal mapping is \[P_y^h(\eta g;\psi):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\left\{\eta\langle g,x\rangle+\eta\psi(x)+D_h(x,y)\right\}.\] It is set-valued unless existence and uniqueness are ensured.
