children.title: Trajectory Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failures of smooth-descent intuition and pointwise trajectory behavior.

children.title: Non-Descent Subgradient Directions
children.top_down_role: Valid subgradient directions that do not yield local objective descent.

assumptions_latex: At \(x=0\), select the valid subgradient \(g=1\in\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t>0\), \(f(0-tg)=t>0=f(0)\); hence \(-g\) is not a descent direction.

notation.meaning: Selected subgradient at the current point.

review_flags: The provisional section concerns descent directions; confirm that it supports the convex-subgradient distinction used here.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional convex example at a nonsmooth minimizer.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Descent Directions p. 120
source_refs.source_title: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), the point \(x=0\) minimizes \(f\), and \(g=1\) is a valid member of \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\). Nevertheless, the conventional subgradient direction \(-g=-1\) is not a local descent direction: for every \(t>0\), one has \(f(0-tg)=|-t|=t>0=f(0)\). Thus validity of the subgradient inequality alone does not imply descent along the negative selected subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute-value function at zero, choosing subgradient one is valid, but every positive step in its negative direction strictly increases the objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Descent Subgradient Directions

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Descent Directions p. 120
source_witnesses.source_title: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Descent Test for a Selected Convex Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp criterion for whether the negative selected subgradient is a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be finite and convex on a neighborhood of \(x\), and let \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Then \(f'(x;-g)=\max_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,-g\rangle=-\min_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,g\rangle\). Consequently, \(-g\) is a strict descent direction if and only if \(\min_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,g\rangle>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative selected subgradient is a strict descent direction exactly when every subgradient has positive inner product with that selection.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and convex on a neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -g\text{ is a strict descent direction}\iff\min_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,g\rangle>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Descent Test for a Selected Convex Subgradient

children.title: Objective Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Nonmonotone objective behavior along ordinary subgradient trajectories.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates alternate between \(\alpha/3\) and \(-2\alpha/3\), so objective values alternate between \(\alpha/3\) and \(2\alpha/3\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports this constant-stepsize oscillation example.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact two-cycle for the ordinary constant-stepsize subgradient method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=|x|\) and the constant-stepsize update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) for nonzero iterates, where \(\alpha>0\). Starting from \(x_0=\alpha/3\) gives \(x_1=-2\alpha/3\) and \(x_2=\alpha/3\), so the trajectory repeats with period two. Accordingly, \(f(x_{2j})=\alpha/3\) and \(f(x_{2j+1})=2\alpha/3\), demonstrating that valid subgradient updates need not produce a monotone or convergent objective sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-step method on the absolute-value function can enter a two-cycle whose objective values alternate forever instead of decreasing monotonically.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Oscillation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated two-cycle and alternating objective values are mathematically correct and fit the objective-oscillation container, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the example.

children.title: Value Convergence without Iterate Convergence
children.top_down_role: Objective progress without convergence of the raw trajectory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient Trajectory with Convergent Values and Two Limit Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A genuine convex subgradient trajectory whose values converge optimally while its iterates do not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,[-1,1])=\max\{|x|-1,0\}\), and let \(\varepsilon_k>0\) satisfy \(\varepsilon_k\to0\). Set \(x_k=(-1)^k(1+\varepsilon_k)\), choose \(g_k=(-1)^k\in\partial f(x_k)\), and take \(\alpha_k=2+\varepsilon_k+\varepsilon_{k+1}\). Then \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\), \(f(x_k)=\varepsilon_k\to0=f^*\), while \(x_{2k}\to1\) and \(x_{2k+1}\to-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid subgradient trajectory can alternate near two minimizers while its objective values converge to the optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Trajectory with Convergent Values and Two Limit Points

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness and Boundedness Upgrade Value Convergence to Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient conditions excluding this failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous with unique minimizer \(x^*\). If \((x_k)\) is bounded and \(f(x_k)\to f(x^*)\), then \(x_k\to x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous objective with a unique minimizer, boundedness upgrades objective-value convergence to convergence of the points.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness and Boundedness Upgrade Value Convergence to Iterate Convergence

assumptions_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be the constant convex function \(f(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f(x_k)=f^*=0\) for every \(k\), the sequence \((x_k)\) has no limit.
review_flags: The example establishes the logical failure boundary for value convergence but is not itself an unconstrained subgradient-update trajectory.
No supplied locator directly supports the intended trajectory-level formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation of objective-value convergence from convergence of points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Objective-value convergence alone does not imply convergence of the underlying points. Indeed, for the convex function \(f(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the bounded sequence \(x_k=(-1)^k\) satisfies \(f(x_k)=0=f^*\) for every \(k\), while \((x_k)\) does not converge. Therefore a theorem upgrading \(f(x_k)\to f^*\) to iterate convergence needs additional structure, such as uniqueness of the minimizer together with suitable compactness or trajectory control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an optimal objective value at every index does not force the points to converge when the minimizer set contains multiple points.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Convergence without Iterate Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example proves only that objective-value convergence does not imply convergence of an arbitrary point sequence. Because the immutable context is a trajectory failure boundary for convex subgradient methods, the sequence must arise from an applicable subgradient trajectory or the claim must be supported by a source establishing the intended trajectory-level phenomenon. The present record does neither.

children.title: Ergodic–Pointwise Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Certified averaged outputs despite weak or absent pointwise progress.

assumptions_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\), choose \(a>0\), and use the fixed stepsize \(2a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every even horizon \(T=2m\), the average \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k=0\) is optimal, while \(f(x_k)=a>0\) for every raw iterate.
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly treats ergodic versus pointwise subgradient guarantees.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact averaging gap produced by a symmetric two-cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-2a\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) with \(a>0\) and \(x_0=a\). The raw iterates alternate as \(x_k=(-1)^ka\), and hence \(f(x_k)=a\) at every iteration. For each even horizon \(T=2m\), however, the uniform average satisfies \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k=0\), so \(f(\bar x_T)=0=f^*\). An exact ergodic certificate can therefore coexist with absent pointwise objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric two-cycle stays uniformly suboptimal at every raw iterate, while each even-horizon average is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic–Pointwise Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric two-cycle and its even-horizon average are computed correctly, and the counterexample fits the ergodic-pointwise mismatch container. No cited source supports this trajectory-level distinction, however.

children.title: Stepsize Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns caused by persistent, overly rapid, or incorrectly targeted policies.

children.title: Constant-Stepsize Accuracy Floor
children.top_down_role: Persistent neighborhood behavior under a fixed scale.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant Raw-Stepsize Accuracy Floor and Sharp Two-Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon best-iterate bound and exact one-dimensional realization of its persistent term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k)\), where \(\alpha>0\), \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\|g_k\|\le G\). Then, for every \(T\ge1\), \[\min_{0\le k<T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\le \frac{\|x_0-x^*\|^2}{2\alpha T}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}.\] The persistent term is sharp: for \(f(x)=G|x|\) and \(x_0=\alpha G/2\), the unique nonzero-iterate selections \(g_k=G\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) give \[x_k=(-1)^k\frac{\alpha G}{2},\qquad f(x_k)-f^*=\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}\quad(k\ge0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed raw subgradient multiplier gives a vanishing transient plus an alpha-times-G-squared-over-two floor, and the absolute-value objective attains that floor in an exact two-cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), and a minimizer \(x^*\in C\) exists.
The method uses a fixed raw multiplier \(\alpha>0\) and selected subgradients satisfying \(\|g_k\|\le G\).
The sharpness example is unconstrained with \(f(x)=G|x|\) and \(x_0=\alpha G/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The best-iterate gap has the bound \(\|x_0-x^*\|^2/(2\alpha T)+\alpha G^2/2\), and the persistent term cannot be reduced uniformly under these assumptions.

notation.meaning: Fixed multiplier applied to the raw subgradient.
Uniform norm bound for the selected subgradients.

review_flags: replaces_deferred_seed: retains the standard bound and adds a sharp local two-cycle
knowledge_statements.title: Constant Raw-Stepsize Accuracy Floor and Sharp Two-Cycle

assumptions_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex on closed convex \(C\), with a minimizer \(x^*\in C\).
Use \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k)\), where \(\alpha>0\), \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lVert g_k\rVert\leq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(T\geq1\), \(\min_{0\leq k<T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\leq\frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{2\alpha T}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}\), leaving the persistent floor \(\alpha G^2/2\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the standard projected-subgradient constant-stepsize bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate objective bound for projected Euclidean subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For projected subgradient descent with a constant stepsize \(\alpha>0\), convexity and nonexpansiveness of projection yield the finite-horizon guarantee \[\min_{0\leq k<T}\bigl(f(x_k)-f^*\bigr)\leq \frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{2\alpha T}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}.\] Thus increasing \(T\) removes the initial-distance term but not the additive term \(\alpha G^2/2\). Without decreasing \(\alpha\) or imposing stronger structure, this guarantee certifies approach only to a fixed objective neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded subgradients and a fixed step, the best objective gap has a vanishing transient plus a persistent term proportional to the stepsize.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Stepsize Accuracy Floor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The best-iterate constant-stepsize bound is standard, correctly stated under the listed convexity, projection, minimizer, and bounded-subgradient hypotheses, and complexity_bound is the appropriate role. It nevertheless lacks a source with a specific theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Prematurely Summable Stepsizes
children.top_down_role: Insufficient cumulative motion under overly rapid decay.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Travel Budget of Summable Displacements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric obstruction underlying failure from premature summability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\), suppose \(L:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k\lVert g_k\rVert<\infty\). Then \(\lVert x_k-x_0\rVert\le L\), and for every nonempty solution set \(X^*\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\ge\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)-L\). Thus if \(\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)>L\), no iterate reaches \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable realized step lengths give only a finite travel budget, so a more distant solution set cannot be reached.
assumptions_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\) in a normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Travel Budget of Summable Displacements

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subgradient iterates satisfy \(x_k=x_0-\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i>0\) and converge to \(x_0-S>0\), which is not optimal.
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports this summable-stepsize failure example.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp one-dimensional failure caused by finite cumulative stepsize.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), suppose \(\alpha_k>0\) and \(S:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k<\infty\). Choose \(x_0>S\) and apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\) with \(g_k=1\), which remains the unique subgradient while \(x_k>0\). Then \(x_k=x_0-\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i\) and \(x_k\to x_0-S>0\). The finite cumulative motion cannot reach the minimizer \(0\), despite valid subgradients and vanishing stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If positive steps sum to a finite distance, an absolute-value iterate started farther away can stop short of the minimizer forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Prematurely Summable Stepsizes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The summable-stepsize construction is correct and exactly demonstrates insufficient cumulative motion, but no source with an inspectable locator supports the failure example.

children.title: Misestimated Polyak Target
children.top_down_role: Failure or stagnation caused by unreliable objective-level information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Underestimated Polyak Target Produces a Persistent Two-Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of a target strictly below the optimum in the untruncated Polyak rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\), \(\widehat f=-\delta<f^*=0\), and \(g_k=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) at nonzero iterates. With \(\alpha_k=(f(x_k)-\widehat f)/\lVert g_k\rVert^2=|x_k|+\delta\), every \(x_0\ne0\) satisfies \(x_1=-\delta\operatorname{sign}(x_0)\) and \(x_{k+1}=-x_k\) thereafter. Hence \(f(x_k)-f^*=\delta\) for all \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Polyak target below the optimum can force the absolute-value method into a permanent two-cycle at a gap equal to the target error.
assumptions_latex: The untruncated Polyak update selects \(g_k=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) at nonzero iterates.

notation.meaning: Target used by the Polyak rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Underestimated Polyak Target Produces a Persistent Two-Cycle

assumptions_latex: Use the Polyak-form update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{f(x_k)-\widehat f}{\lVert g_k\rVert^2}g_k\) with an estimate \(\widehat f=c>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For any \(x_0\in(0,c)\) and \(g_k=1\), one obtains \(x_1=c\) and thereafter \(x_k=c\), so the method stagnates at objective gap \(c\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports failure from an overestimated Polyak target.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overestimated target causing a negative step followed by nonoptimal stagnation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(f(x)=|x|\), choose an estimated target \(\widehat f=c>f^*=0\), and initialize \(x_0\in(0,c)\). With \(g_0=1\), the nominal Polyak stepsize is \(\alpha_0=f(x_0)-c=x_0-c<0\), giving \(x_1=x_0-\alpha_0=c\). At \(x_k=c\), selecting \(g_k=1\) gives \(\alpha_k=f(c)-c=0\), hence \(x_{k+1}=c\). The erroneous target therefore causes an ascent move and permanent stagnation at positive objective gap \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An estimated target above the true optimum can make a Polyak step move away and then stagnate forever at the incorrect target level.
knowledge_statements.title: Misestimated Polyak Target

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebra is correct for the displayed untruncated Polyak-form update: an overestimated target produces a negative nominal stepsize, followed by stagnation at x=c. Because standard Polyak policies commonly require a valid lower target or enforce nonnegative stepsizes, a source is needed to establish the exact convention and claimed failure boundary.

children.title: Geometry-Implementation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limitations caused by unavailable radius control, poor geometry, or expensive feasibility operations.

children.title: Unbounded Domain without Radius Control
children.top_down_role: Absence of a finite comparison radius or divergence bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon bound isolating the comparison-radius parameter absent from an uncontrolled unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\|g_k\|\le G\), and \(\alpha_k>0\). For every \(x^*\in\arg\min_C f\), \[\min_{0\le k<T}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)\le \frac{\|x_0-x^*\|^2+G^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2}{2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k}.\] Thus unboundedness does not invalidate the per-comparator bound, but no class-uniform accuracy follows without a uniform bound on \(\|x_0-x^*\|\) or equivalent trajectory control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected-subgradient accuracy depends on the initial distance to an optimizer; an unbounded domain prevents a uniform guarantee when that distance is uncontrolled.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(f\) is convex on \(C\) and attains its minimum at \(x^*\in C\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set.
Uniform bound on selected subgradient norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius-Dependent Projected-Subgradient Bound

assumptions_latex: Fix \(G>0\) and consider the family \(f_a(x)=G|x-a|\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), indexed by \(a\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although every \(f_a\) has subgradients bounded by \(G\), the comparison radius is \(R_a=|a|\), which is unbounded over the family; therefore bounds depending only on \(G\) cannot provide a uniform finite accuracy guarantee.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports radius dependence in convex subgradient oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation family exposing the missing initial-distance parameter on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the unbounded domain \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(f_a(x)=G|x-a|\) and start at \(x_0=0\). Each function is convex, has minimum value \(0\) at \(x^*=a\), and admits subgradients of norm at most \(G\). However, the comparison radius is \(R_a=\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert=|a|\), which can be arbitrarily large. Consequently, a complexity statement uniform over this family cannot eliminate dependence on an initial-distance, bounded-level-set, or equivalent trajectory-control parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded subgradients alone give no uniform radius: translating an absolute-value minimizer arbitrarily far away makes the usual distance-dependent complexity unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Domain without Radius Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translation family correctly shows that bounded subgradients do not bound the initial comparison radius. The stronger conclusion about absence of a uniform finite accuracy guarantee depends on the oracle information and algorithm class, neither of which is specified or sourced, so the complexity implication cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Mirror Geometry
children.top_down_role: Mirror choices whose geometric constants erase their intended advantage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative loss caused by poor scaling of a smooth strongly convex mirror map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose mirror descent uses a differentiable mirror function \(h\) that is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex and \(L_h\)-smooth relative to the chosen norm on \(C\). If \(\|g_k\|_*\le G\) and an optimizer \(x^*\) satisfies \(\|x^*-x_1\|\le R\), the constant-step ergodic estimate gives \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le G\sqrt{\frac{2D_h(x^*,x_1)}{\sigma T}}\le GR\sqrt{\frac{L_h}{\sigma T}}.\] Thus the mirror condition number \(\kappa_h=L_h/\sigma\) enters as \(\sqrt{\kappa_h}\), and a poorly scaled mirror map can erase its intended geometric advantage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Poor mirror scaling inflates the standard ergodic bound by the square root of the mirror condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(h\) is differentiable, \(\sigma\)-strongly convex, and \(L_h\)-smooth on the relevant region.

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the mirror function.
Condition number of the mirror geometry relative to the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror Condition-Number Degradation

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space.
The mirror function \(h\) is differentiable, \(\sigma\)-strongly convex, and \(L_h\)-smooth on \(C\).
Selected subgradients satisfy \(\lVert g_k\rVert_*\le G\), and \(\lVert x^-x_1\rVert\le R\) for an optimizer \(x^\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the mirror function.
Condition number of the mirror geometry relative to the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constant-step mirror descent, the standard estimate is \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^)\le \frac{D_h(x^,x_1)}{\eta T}+\frac{\eta G^2}{2\sigma}.\] Optimizing \(\eta\) gives \(G\sqrt{2D_h(x^,x_1)/(\sigma T)}\). Since \(L_h\)-smoothness implies \(D_h(x^,x_1)\le L_hR^2/2\), the bound becomes \(GR\sqrt{\kappa_h/T}\). Thus a mirror map with large \(\kappa_h=L_h/\sigma\) may have a nominally favorable shape while its geometric constants erase the improvement over a well-scaled Euclidean geometry.

children.title: Intractable Projection or Prox Mapping
children.top_down_role: Favorable oracle counts paired with prohibitive per-iteration subproblems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer Oracle Counts Do Not Bound Total Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of projection-or-prox call complexity from end-to-end computational cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an outer method requires \(T(\varepsilon)\) projection or proximal evaluations to reach accuracy \(\varepsilon\), and the \(k\)-th required subproblem costs \(C_k\). Then \[\operatorname{Work}(\varepsilon)\ge\sum_{k=0}^{T(\varepsilon)-1}C_k.\] Consequently a favorable outer oracle count does not imply a tractable algorithm when exact mapping evaluation is intractable or the required approximation accuracy cannot be obtained efficiently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small outer iteration count gives no end-to-end efficiency guarantee when each projection or proximal subproblem is prohibitively expensive.
assumptions_latex: The outer method requires \(T(\varepsilon)\) projection or proximal evaluations.
The computational cost of the \(k\)-th required mapping evaluation is \(C_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Work}(\varepsilon)\ge\sum_{k<T(\varepsilon)}C_k\), so unit-cost oracle complexity alone does not establish tractability.

notation.meaning: Number of outer mapping calls required for accuracy epsilon.
Cost of the projection or proximal subproblem at iteration k.

notation.meaning: Number of outer oracle iterations required for accuracy epsilon.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates outer oracle complexity from end-to-end computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an outer method calls either \(P_C(z)=\arg\min_{x\in C}\lVert x-z\rVert^2/2\) or \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda r}(z)=\arg\min_x\{r(x)+\lVert x-z\rVert^2/(2\lambda)\}\) once per iteration. An iteration bound \(T(\varepsilon)\) counts these calls as unit-cost operations. The actual work is at least \(\sum_{k<T(\varepsilon)}C_k\), where \(C_k\) is the cost of solving the required subproblem. If exact evaluation is intractable or the necessary approximation accuracy cannot be achieved efficiently, the favorable outer oracle count does not imply an efficient algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small iteration count is not meaningful when each required projection or proximal subproblem is computationally prohibitive.
knowledge_statements.title: Intractable Projection or Prox Mapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implementation-cost boundary and content kind fit the container, but the record supplies no inspectable citation for its tractability claim.

children.title: Oracle Information Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Information defects that weaken guarantees or remove common output mechanisms.

children.title: Persistent Deterministic Oracle Error
children.top_down_role: Nonvanishing bias or approximation error in oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon bound and sharp nonvanishing floor for deterministic projected subgradient descent with a uniform additive support error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\widetilde g_k\) satisfies \[f(y)\ge f(x_k)+\langle\widetilde g_k,y-x_k\rangle-\delta\quad(y\in C),\qquad \|\widetilde g_k\|\le G,\] and \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k\widetilde g_k)\). If \(\|x_1-x^*\|\le R\), then \[\min_{1\le k\le T}(f(x_k)-f^*)\le \frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k=1}^T\alpha_k^2}{2\sum_{k=1}^T\alpha_k}+\delta.\] The floor is sharp: for \(f(x)=G|x|\), \(x_1=\delta/G\), and the valid response \(\widetilde g_k=0\), every iterate remains at \(x_1\) with \(f(x_k)-f^*=\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent deterministic delta-subgradient error adds a delta floor to the standard objective-gap bound, and a one-dimensional valid oracle can attain that floor forever.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), and a minimizer \(x^*\in C\) exists.
Every response is a convex \(\delta\)-subgradient with the same \(\delta\ge0\) and satisfies \(\|\widetilde g_k\|\le G\).
The stepsizes are positive and \(\|x_1-x^*\|\le R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The best-iterate guarantee contains an unavoidable additive \(\delta\) term in general.

notation.meaning: Uniform additive defect in the global convex support inequality.

review_flags: replaces_deferred_seed: corrects optimizer and optimal-value notation and includes a sharp local counterexample
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Additive Oracle-Error Floor

assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex on a closed convex set \(C\).
At iteration \(k\), the oracle returns a \(\delta\)-subgradient \(\tilde g_k\) with \(\lVert\tilde g_k\rVert\le G\).

notation.meaning: Persistent additive error in the subgradient inequality.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard projected inexact-subgradient recursion with a uniform additive oracle error.
source_locator_needed: No supplied locator directly supports the deterministic error-floor formula.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform additive-error model for deterministic projected subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the oracle inequality \[f(y)\ge f(x_k)+\langle\tilde g_k,y-x_k\rangle-\delta\qquad\text{for every }y\in C\] holds with fixed \(\delta>0\), and set \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k\tilde g_k)\). Then the usual distance recursion yields \[\min_{1\le k\le T}\bigl(f(x_k)-f^\bigr)\le \frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k=1}^T\alpha_k^2}{2\sum_{k=1}^T\alpha_k}+\delta.\] Even when the stepsize-dependent term tends to zero, persistent deterministic error prevents this guarantee from establishing objective accuracy below \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic additive oracle error that does not vanish produces a matching nonzero floor in the standard objective-gap guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Deterministic Oracle Error

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-error floor is standard and locally appropriate, but the exact deterministic bound lacks a source; \(x^\) and \(f^\) are also malformed.

children.title: Uncontrolled Subgradient Selection
children.top_down_role: Adverse selection among valid but poorly scaled subgradients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniform subgradient guarantees when the oracle may choose arbitrarily large valid elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), the basic projected-subgradient estimate contains \(\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_*^2\); hence a bound with constant \(G\) requires \(\|g_k\|_*\le G\) for the responses actually selected. Mere nonemptiness of \(\partial f(x_k)\) is insufficient. For example, \[f(x)=x+\delta_{[0,\infty)}(x)\] is proper closed convex, has unique minimizer \(x^*=0\), and satisfies \(\partial f(0)=(-\infty,1]\). For any \(M>0\), the valid choice \(g_0=-M\) in the unconstrained extended-real update gives \[x_1=\alpha M,\qquad f(x_1)-f(x^*)=\alpha M.\] Thus valid selection at an optimizer can cause an arbitrarily large excursion and objective increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rate needs a bound on the subgradients actually returned; an unbounded boundary subdifferential permits arbitrarily bad valid selections even at an optimizer.
assumptions_latex: The oracle may return any member of the current convex subdifferential without a norm-control rule.
The displayed example uses the raw unconstrained update for an extended-real objective with domain \([0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonemptiness of the subdifferential alone gives no uniform displacement or objective-gap guarantee over all valid selections.

notation.meaning: Dual norm associated with the update geometry.
Convex indicator of the nonnegative half-line.
Arbitrarily large magnitude of the adverse selected subgradient.

review_flags: replaces_deferred_seed: adds a precise adverse-selection family showing that the selected-norm hypothesis cannot be replaced by subdifferential nonemptiness
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Selected-Subgradient Boundary

assumptions_latex: The oracle may return any element of \(\partial f(x_k)\), without a prescribed selection rule or norm bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(\sup_k\lVert g_k\rVert_*<\infty\), the standard subgradient complexity estimate has no finite uniform constant and may be vacuous.

notation.meaning: Subgradient selected by the oracle at iteration k.
Dual norm associated with the update geometry.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard subgradient rates require control of the norms of the actually selected oracle responses.
source_locator_needed: A source is needed for a precise adverse-selection example or theorem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary caused by unbounded norms of the selected, rather than merely existing, subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the update \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), the basic recursion contains the positive term \(\alpha_k^2\lVert g_k\rVert_*^2\). Consequently, a rate expressed through a constant \(G\) requires \(\lVert g_k\rVert_*\le G\) for the subgradients actually returned. The weaker condition \(\partial f(x_k)\ne\varnothing\) is insufficient: if the oracle may choose elements of arbitrarily large norm from these sets, then \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2\lVert g_k\rVert_*^2\) need not be controlled, and the usual bounded-subgradient convergence and complexity conclusions do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existence of valid subgradients is insufficient when the oracle can select arbitrarily large ones; the standard rate constant then becomes uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Subgradient Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected-subgradient norm boundary is appropriate, but an authoritative source or precise adverse-selection result is required.

children.title: Missing or Unreliable Objective Values
children.top_down_role: Loss of best-iterate, target-level, and direct value-gap mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of value-dependent output, stepsize, stopping, and objective-gap mechanisms under a subgradient-only oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the oracle returns query points and valid subgradients \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) but no trustworthy values \(f(x_k)\), and suppose no certified reference level is independently available. Then one cannot evaluate \[k_T\in\arg\min_{1\le k\le T}f(x_k),\qquad f(x_k)\le f_{\mathrm{tar}}+\varepsilon,\qquad \alpha_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f^*}{\|g_k\|^2},\] or directly verify \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\). Predetermined value-free stepsizes and averaging rules remain implementable, and their a priori analysis is not invalidated merely by the absence of observed values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without trustworthy objective values or an independently certified reference level, best-value selection, target tests, Polyak steps, and directly checked objective gaps are unavailable, although predetermined value-free schedules remain possible.
assumptions_latex: The oracle supplies valid subgradients but no reliable objective values.
No independently certified target, optimal value, or lower bound sufficient for the displayed mechanisms is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Value-dependent selection, adaptation, stopping, and direct objective-gap certification cannot be implemented under the stipulated oracle, while predetermined value-free schemes remain implementable.

notation.meaning: Prescribed objective target used by a value-based stopping rule.
Optimal objective value used by an exact Polyak step or gap test.

review_flags: replaces_deferred_seed: corrects malformed optimal-value and best-index notation
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Free Oracle Information Boundary

assumptions_latex: The method receives query points and subgradients but no reliable values of \(f\).
No independently certified lower bound on \(f^\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Best-value selection, target-level tests, Polyak stepsizes, and directly checkable objective-gap certificates are unavailable under this oracle interface.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Each listed mechanism explicitly requires objective values or a certified target/lower bound.
source_locator_needed: No supplied locator formalizes the information limitation of the value-free oracle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for otherwise deterministic convex subgradient methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the oracle supplies only \((x_k,g_k)\) with \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), then the rule \(k^\in\arg\min_{i\le k}f(x_i)\) cannot be evaluated. Likewise, a target-level stopping test \(f(x_k)\le f_{\mathrm{tar}}+\varepsilon\), the Polyak step \(\alpha_k=(f(x_k)-f^)/\lVert g_k\rVert^2\), and the certificate \(f(x_k)-f^\le\varepsilon\) are undefined without reliable values and the required reference level. Value-free schedules and predetermined averaging may remain valid, but these value-dependent selection, adaptation, and certification mechanisms do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without trustworthy objective values, the method loses best-iterate selection, target tests, Polyak steps, and direct verification of an objective gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Unreliable Objective Values

children.title: Method-Scope Transitions

children.title: Cutting-Plane Bundle-Method Transition
children.top_down_role: Persistent model memory and stabilized lower-model methods.

children.title: Cutting-Plane Transition
children.top_down_role: Transition toward methods retaining multiple separating or supporting cuts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact full-memory Kelley convergence under compactness and uniformly bounded oracle subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run the full-memory Kelley method by minimizing \(m_k=\max_{i\le k}\{f(x_i)+\langle g_i,\cdot-x_i\rangle\}\) over \(C\), querying an exact subgradient at each model minimizer, and retaining every cut. If \(C\) is compact, \(f\) is convex and continuous on \(C\), and the returned subgradients satisfy \(\|g_i\|\le G\), then for \(u_k=\min_{i\le k}f(x_i)\) and \(\ell_k=\min_Cm_k\), \[0\le u_k-f^*\le u_k-\ell_k\longrightarrow0.\] Every accumulation point of incumbent query points is therefore optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain with bounded exact subgradients, full-memory Kelley cutting planes drive the certified upper–lower gap to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
Every query returns an exact value and subgradient \(g_i\) with \(\|g_i\|\le G\); every master is solved exactly and all cuts are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_k-\ell_k\to0\), and every incumbent accumulation point belongs to \(\arg\min_C f\).

notation.meaning: Best queried objective value through iteration k.
Minimum value of the retained cutting-plane model.

review_flags: The bounded-subgradient assumption is retained to exclude boundary regimes in which compactness and continuity alone do not control the generated cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Kelley Cutting-Plane Gap Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex and finite on a nonempty compact convex set \(C\).
Each query returns both \(f(x_i)\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cutting-plane model gives a certified lower bound \(\ell_k\le f^\), and each new query globally refines the retained lower model.

notation.meaning: Maximum of the accumulated affine minorants.
Current lower bound obtained by minimizing the model.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Classical Kelley cutting-plane construction for convex minimization.
source_locator_needed: No supplied locator directly covers convex cutting-plane methods.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical value-and-subgradient cutting-plane transition on a compact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with any \(x_1\in C\). After queries \((x_i,f(x_i),g_i)\), define \[m_k(x)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\{f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\}.\] Compute \(x_{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}m_k(x)\) and \(\ell_k=m_k(x_{k+1})\), query the oracle at \(x_{k+1}\), and append the resulting cut. Stop when an available incumbent \(u_k=\min_{i\le k}f(x_i)\) satisfies \(u_k-ell_k\le\varepsilon\); output its attaining query point. Convexity ensures \(m_k(x)\le f(x)\) on \(C\), hence \(\ell_k\le f^\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cutting-plane methods retain affine subgradient cuts, minimize their maximum, and use the resulting lower bound with the best observed value as a certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Transition

children.title: Bundle-Method Transition
children.top_down_role: Transition toward stabilized methods built from persistent lower-model collections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate furnished by a globally valid bundle model that is exact at its stability center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\le f\) on \(C\), let \(m(c)=f(c)\), and define \[y=\arg\min_{x\in C}\left\{m(x)+\frac{1}{2t}\|x-c\|^2\right\},\qquad \delta=f(c)-m(y)-\frac{1}{2t}\|y-c\|^2.\] Then \(\delta\ge0\) and \[0\le f(c)-\min_{x\in C}\left\{f(x)+\frac{1}{2t}\|x-c\|^2\right\}\le\delta.\] In particular, \(\delta=0\) implies that \(c\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a valid model exact at the center, predicted decrease bounds the center's proximal optimality gap, and zero predicted decrease certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(f\) and \(m\) are proper closed convex functions, \(m\le f\) on \(C\), and \(m(c)=f(c)<\infty\).
\(t>0\), and the displayed stabilized model problem has minimizer \(y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Bundle Predicted-Decrease Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex on a closed convex set \(C\).
A bundle of valid affine minorants and reliable objective values is maintained.
The stabilization parameter satisfies \(t_k>0\), and the acceptance fraction satisfies \(\rho\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration either moves the center after sufficient actual decrease or retains it while strengthening the model with a null step.

notation.meaning: Current serious iterate, or stability center.
Piecewise-affine lower model formed from the retained bundle.
Trial point produced by the stabilized model subproblem.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Canonical proximal bundle serious-step/null-step template.
source_locator_needed: No supplied locator directly supports the stated bundle-method transition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic proximal bundle template with serious and null steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given center \(c_k\), model \(m_k\le f\), and \(t_k>0\), compute \[y_k\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\left\{m_k(x)+\frac{1}{2t_k}\lVert x-c_k\rVert^2\right\}.\] Query \(f(y_k)\) and \(g_k\in\partial f(y_k)\), and set \(d_k=f(c_k)-m_k(y_k)\). If \(f(c_k)-f(y_k)\ge\rho d_k\), take a serious step \(c_{k+1}=y_k\); otherwise take a null step \(c_{k+1}=c_k\). In both cases, add the cut generated at \(y_k\), update the bundle, and stop when a prescribed model-gap test is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bundle method stabilizes the cutting-plane model, moves its center only after sufficient decrease, and otherwise uses a null step to improve the model.
knowledge_statements.title: Bundle-Method Transition

children.title: Persistent Model Memory
children.top_down_role: Need for retaining oracle information beyond the current subgradient.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage and direct evaluation cost for dense, uncompressed persistent cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one dense affine cut in \(\mathbb R^n\) is appended per oracle call and none is deleted or aggregated, then after \(k\) calls the model contains \(k\) cuts, requires \(\Theta(kn)\) scalar storage, and direct evaluation of all cut values costs \(\Theta(kn)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense full-memory model grows linearly with the query count in both storage and direct model-evaluation work.
assumptions_latex: One dense affine cut is stored per call, without deletion, aggregation, compression, or exploitable sparsity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(k\) calls, storage and direct model-evaluation work are both \(\Theta(kn)\).
review_flags: Dense uncompressed representation model only; master-solution complexity is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Memory Representation Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Interpolation of Retained Query Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-preservation property of exact persistent convex cutting-plane memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i(x)=f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\), where \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), and let \(m_k=\max_{i\in I_k}a_i\). If every queried index \(j\le k\) remains in \(I_k\), then \[m_k(x_j)=f(x_j)\qquad(j\le k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping every exact supporting cut makes the model agree with the objective at every retained query point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and finite at the query points.
\(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), and every queried cut through iteration k is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k(x_j)=f(x_j)\) for every retained query index \(j\le k\).

notation.meaning: Affine supporting cut generated at query i.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Interpolation of Retained Query Points

assumptions_latex: Every stored pair satisfies \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for a convex function \(f\).
Previously retained cuts are not discarded when the model is updated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[m_k(x)\le m_{k+1}(x)\le f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x,\] so persistent memory monotonically strengthens the global lower model.

notation.meaning: Affine minorant generated by query i.
Maximum of all cuts retained through iteration k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Immediate model property of nested collections of valid convex subgradient cuts.
source_locator_needed: No supplied locator directly treats persistent cutting-plane or bundle memory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact persistence of valid affine cuts; aggregation or deletion requires separate safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each query, let \(a_i(x)=f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\), and let \(m_k(x)=\max_{i\in I_k}a_i(x)\). If the index sets are nested, \(I_k\subseteq I_{k+1}\), then convexity gives \(a_i(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\) and every retained index. Therefore \[m_k(x)\le m_{k+1}(x)\le f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x.\] Persistent model memory thus preserves all accumulated global first-order information and monotonically improves the lower approximation, although the growing bundle may increase storage and subproblem cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retaining every valid cut makes the lower model increase monotonically while remaining below the objective, at the cost of a growing bundle.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Model Memory

children.title: Lower-Model Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Need for controlling trial points generated from accumulated lower models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and exact optimality conditions for the stabilization primitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(m:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}m\ne\varnothing\). For \(c\in C\) and \(t>0\), \[y=\arg\min_{x\in C}\left\{m(x)+\frac{1}{2t}\|x-c\|^2\right\}\] exists and is unique, and \[0\in\partial(m+\delta_C)(y)+\frac1t(y-c).\] If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}m)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\), this becomes \[0\in\partial m(y)+N_C(y)+\frac1t(y-c).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex lower model with nonempty feasible domain has a unique quadratically stabilized minimizer; the split normal-cone condition requires the standard relative-interior qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(m\) is proper, closed, and convex; and \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}m\ne\varnothing\).
\(c\in C\) and \(t>0\); the split subdifferential formula additionally assumes \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}m)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stabilized problem has a unique minimizer satisfying the stated composite optimality inclusion, with the split inclusion under relative-interior qualification.

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the feasible set.
Convex normal cone to C at y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stabilized Master Values Are Not Global Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes trial-point stabilization from certification of the original optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when \(m\le f\), the stabilized value \[q_t(c)=\min_{x\in C}\left\{m(x)+\frac{1}{2t}\|x-c\|^2\right\}\] need not satisfy \(q_t(c)\le f^*\), because the quadratic changes the minimized objective. For \(C=\mathbb R\), \(f=m=|x|\), \(c=1\), and \(0<t<1\), \[q_t(c)=1-\frac t2>0=f^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic stabilization controls the model minimizer but destroys the unstabilized master's global-lower-bound interpretation.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(m\) is a proper closed convex model satisfying \(m\le f\), and \(t>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a center \(c_k\in C\), define the stabilized model problem \[y_k=\arg\min_{x\in C}\left\{m_k(x)+\frac{1}{2t_k}\lVert x-c_k\rVert^2\right\}.\] In a Euclidean space, the quadratic term makes the objective strongly convex, so the minimizer is unique whenever it exists. knowledge_statements.title: Transition to Proximal Composite Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex forward-backward splitting for a smooth-plus-proximable objective on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}r\) and choose \(0<\alpha\le 1/L\). Proximal gradient iterates according to \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha r}\bigl(x_k-\alpha\nabla F(x_k)\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\alpha r}(z)=\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{r(x)+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert x-z\rVert^2\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(x_{k+1}\) minimizes the quadratic upper model of \(F\) at \(x_k\) plus \(r\). This transition exploits the smooth-plus-proximable structure instead of treating the entire objective as a black-box nonsmooth function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a convex objective splits into a smooth term with Lipschitz gradient and a proximable convex term, proximal gradient directly exploits that structure.

\(r:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and has a computable proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0<\alpha\le 1/L\), the update \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha r}(x_k-\alpha\nabla F(x_k))\) exploits the smooth-plus-proximable composite structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected finite-horizon objective bound under a conditionally unbiased bounded-second-moment convex subgradient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k=1,\ldots,T\), query \(G_k\), set \[x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha G_k),\qquad \bar x_T=\frac1T\sum_{k=1}^T x_k.\] If \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid x_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\mathbb E[\|G_k\|^2\mid x_k]\le G^2\), and \(\|x_1-x^*\|\le R\), then \[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)]-f^*\le \frac{R^2}{2\alpha T}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}.\] With \(\alpha=R/(G\sqrt T)\), this becomes \[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)]-f^*\le \frac{RG}{\sqrt T}.\]

children.title: Saddle-Point Transition
children.top_down_role: Transition to structured convex-concave formulations with coupled primal-dual variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle inequalities, sectionwise optimality inclusions, and the primal–dual gap for a finite convex–concave problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\). A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point exactly when \[L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\quad( x\in X,\ y\in Y).\] Equivalently, \[0\in \partial_xL(x^*,y^*)+N_X(x^*),\qquad 0\in-\partial_yL(x^*,y^*)+N_Y(y^*).\] Thus, with \(F(x,y)=\partial_xL(x,y)\times(-\partial_yL(x,y))\), saddle points solve \(0\in F(x^*,y^*)+N_{X\times Y}(x^*,y^*)\). If the two marginal extrema are finite, \[\mathcal G(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\ge0,\] and \(\mathcal G(x,y)=0\) exactly when \((x,y)\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave saddle point is equivalently a zero of the sectionwise saddle operator plus the product normal cone; a finite primal–dual gap is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
For every fixed feasible value of the other variable, \(L(\cdot,y)\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and \(-L(x,\cdot)\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex.
The marginal supremum and infimum used in \(\mathcal G\) are finite at candidates where the gap certificate is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \(0\in F(x^*,y^*)+N_{X\times Y}(x^*,y^*)\), and a finite gap satisfies \(\mathcal G(x,y)=0\) if and only if \((x,y)\) is a saddle point.

notation.meaning: Set-valued saddle operator formed from the two sectionwise convex subdifferentials.

For a candidate \((\bar x,\bar y)\), the natural certificate is \[\mathcal G(\bar x,\bar y)=\sup_{y\in Y}L(\bar x,y)-\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\bar y).\]

children.title: Mirror-Prox Transition
children.top_down_role: Transition to non-Euclidean extragradient methods for structured operators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact-oracle rate for the weighted prediction-point output under finite Bregman radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t\) and \(\Omega=\sup_{z\in C}V_{x_1}(z)<\infty\). If \(F\) is monotone and every Mirror-Prox one-step error satisfies \(\Delta_t\le0\), then \[\sup_{z\in C}\frac1{\Gamma_T}\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t\langle F(y_t),y_t-z\rangle\le\frac{\Omega}{\Gamma_T}.\] For \(\bar y_T=\Gamma_T^{-1}\sum_t\gamma_ty_t\), monotonicity consequently gives \[\sup_{z\in C}\langle F(z),\bar y_T-z\rangle\le\frac{\Omega}{\Gamma_T}.\] If \(L>0\) and \(\gamma_t=1/L\), the bound is \(L\Omega/T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-Prox achieves an order-one-over-T ergodic Minty-gap bound for monotone Lipschitz operators with finite Bregman radius.
assumptions_latex: The immutable-seed Mirror-Prox update is used and \(\Delta_t\le0\) at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \sup_{z\in C}\langle F(z),\bar y_T-z\rangle\le\Omega/\Gamma_T\); for \(\gamma_t=1/L\), this is \(L\Omega/T\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stepsize condition making the standard prediction-correction error term nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the distance-generating function is \(1\)-strongly convex and \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the associated primal and dual norms. For Mirror-Prox points \(y_t\) and \(x_{t+1}\), define \[\Delta_t=\gamma_t\langle F(y_t)-F(x_t),y_t-x_{t+1}\rangle-V_{x_t}(y_t)-V_{y_t}(x_{t+1}).\] If \(\gamma_tL\le1\), then \(\Delta_t\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stepsize no larger than the reciprocal Lipschitz constant makes the standard Mirror-Prox one-step error nonpositive.

\(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz from the primal norm to its dual norm.

Mirror-Prox Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic Mirror-Prox with Bregman prox geometry; no convergence rate or computable stopping certificate is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\) and \(g\in E^*\), define \[P_x(g)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\{\langle g,u\rangle+V_x(u)\}.\] Given \(x_1\in C\), for \(t=1,\ldots,T\) compute \[y_t=P_{x_t}(\gamma_tF(x_t)),\qquad x_{t+1}=P_{x_t}(\gamma_tF(y_t)).\] Thus, the operator is evaluated at the current point and at the predicted point, while both proximal steps use the base point \(x_t\). Return the weighted ergodic point \[\bar y_T=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_ty_t}{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-Prox makes a mirror prediction, reevaluates the monotone operator at that prediction, performs a correction from the original base point, and returns the stepsize-weighted average of the prediction points.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional normed vector space with dual \(E^*\), and \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\omega:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and strongly convex, with \(V_x(u)=\omega(u)-\omega(x)-\langle\nabla\omega(x),u-x\rangle\).
\(F:C\to E^*\) is a monotone operator available through point evaluations, and \(\gamma_t>0\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar y_T\) is the stepsize-weighted average of the Mirror-Prox prediction points \(y_t\).

children.title: Monotone-Operator Interface
children.top_down_role: Operator-oriented representation underlying variational or saddle-point problems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-domain scalar certificate for the monotone variational-inequality interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[G_M(z)=\sup_{u\in C}\langle F(u),z-u\rangle.\] If \(C\) is compact and \(F\) is continuous, then \(G_M(z)\) is finite and nonnegative for every \(z\in C\), and \(G_M(z)=0\) exactly when \(z\) solves the Minty variational inequality. If \(F\) is also monotone, the segment continuity already provided by continuity makes this equivalent to the Stampacchia variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain, the nonnegative Minty gap vanishes exactly at monotone variational-inequality solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(F:C\to E\) is continuous; equivalence with the Stampacchia formulation additionally uses monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General monotone-operator formulations underlying the differentiable saddle specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Stampacchia variational inequality is \[\langle F(z^*),z-z^*\rangle\ge0\qquad(\forall z\in C),\] while the Minty variational inequality is \[\langle F(z),z-z^*\rangle\ge0\qquad(\forall z\in C).\] If \(F\) is monotone, every Stampacchia solution is a Minty solution. If \(F\) is additionally continuous along feasible line segments, the two solution sets coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator the usual variational inequality implies the Minty form; continuity along feasible segments makes the formulations equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
For the reverse implication, \(F\) is continuous on each feasible line segment.
knowledge_statements.title: Stampacchia–Minty Variational-Inequality Equivalence
Monotone-Operator Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle problems represented as monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(Z=X\times Y\) and define \[F(x,y)=\bigl(\nabla_x\Phi(x,y),-\nabla_y\Phi(x,y)\bigr).\] Convexity-concavity implies that \(F\) is monotone on \(Z\). A point \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\in Z\) satisfies \[\Phi(x^*,y)\leq\Phi(x^*,y^*)\leq\Phi(x,y^*)\qquad\text{for all }(x,y)\in Z\] if and only if it satisfies \[\langle F(z^*),z-z^*\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for all }z\in Z.\] This representation replaces scalar objective descent by a monotone-operator residual or gap criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable convex-concave saddle problem is equivalently a variational inequality for its monotone saddle-gradient operator, shifting the target from objective decrease to an operator residual or gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
\(\Phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable, convex in its first argument, and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point of \(\Phi\) if and only if \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\) solves the stated variational inequality for \(F\) on \(Z\).

children.title: Extragradient Necessity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where a basic subgradient response is insufficient for the target operator structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cocoercivity Boundary for Stable Forward Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stronger operator regime in which an extra evaluation is unnecessary for unconstrained zero finding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F\) has a zero \(z^*\) and is \(\beta\)-cocoercive: \[\langle F(z)-F(w),z-w\rangle\ge\beta\|F(z)-F(w)\|^2.\] Then the forward iteration \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma F(z_k)\), with \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), satisfies \[\|z_{k+1}-z^*\|^2\le\|z_k-z^*\|^2-\gamma(2\beta-\gamma)\|F(z_k)\|^2.\] Thus the extragradient correction is a general safeguard for monotone-Lipschitz operators lacking such forward-step regularity, not a necessity for every monotone problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward steps are stable under cocoercivity; prediction-correction is needed as a general safeguard when only monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity are known.
review_flags: This is an unconstrained zero-finding boundary; projected forward iterations require their corresponding constrained hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity Boundary for Stable Forward Steps

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forward method diverges in norm, whereas the two-evaluation extragradient method converges linearly to the variational-inequality solution \(0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bilinear rotation isolates the stability failure that motivates an extragradient evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F(z)=Az\) is monotone and \(1\)-Lipschitz, and its unconstrained variational inequality has the unique solution \(z^*=0\). The one-evaluation forward iteration obeys \[z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma Az_k,\qquad \|z_{k+1}\|^2=(1+\gamma^2)\|z_k\|^2,\] so every nonzero trajectory diverges. In contrast, the extragradient update \[y_k=z_k-\gamma Az_k,
\qquad z_{k+1}=z_k-\gamma Ay_k\] satisfies \[\|z_{k+1}\|^2=(1-\gamma^2+\gamma^4)\|z_k\|^2<\|z_k\|^2.\] Hence monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity alone do not ensure stability of a fixed-step forward evaluation; a prediction-correction evaluation can restore contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone rotational operator, a fixed forward step diverges, while extragradient contracts. This exposes a regime where ordinary subgradient-style forward updates are unstable.
knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Necessity Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Stationarity Is Not Convex Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex subgradient optimality and objective-gap reasoning after transition to locally Lipschitz nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), \[\partial_C f(0)=[-1,1],\qquad 0\in\partial_C f(0),\] although \(0\) is a strict global maximum and not a local minimizer. Moreover, the selection \(g=0\) does not satisfy the convex support inequality: for every \(y\ne0\), \[f(y)<f(0)+g(y-0)=0.\] Hence Clarke stationarity alone neither certifies minimality nor supplies the global affine lower bound used in convex averaging and objective-gap complexity arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function minus absolute value is Clarke-stationary at its strict maximum, demonstrating that nonconvex stationarity neither certifies minimality nor preserves convex support and gap arguments.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is the locally Lipschitz nonconvex function \(f(x)=-|x|\).
Stationarity is interpreted through the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_C f(0)\) does not imply local or global minimality, and it does not validate the convex subgradient inequality or the gap analysis derived from that inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Stationarity Is Not Convex Optimality
Transition to Nonconvex Nonsmooth Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex global guarantees under locally Lipschitz nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(\bar x=0\), the Clarke subdifferential is \[\partial_C f(0)=[-1,1],\] so \(0\in\partial_C f(0)\). Nevertheless, \(0\) is a strict local and global maximum rather than a minimizer, because \(f(x)<f(0)=0\) for every \(x\neq0\). Moreover, choosing \(g=0\in\partial_C f(0)\) does not yield the convex subgradient inequality: \[f(y)\geq f(0)+g(y-0)\] fails for every \(y\neq0\). Thus, the convex passage from a subgradient inequality to averaged objective-gap and global oracle-complexity bounds is unavailable; a nonconvex nonsmooth method must instead specify an appropriate stationarity measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconvex nonsmooth function, a zero Clarke subgradient can occur at a strict maximum. It therefore neither certifies global minimality nor supplies the convex subgradient inequality used in averaging and objective-gap analyses.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is the locally Lipschitz nonconvex function \(f(x)=-|x|\).
Stationarity is interpreted using the Clarke subdifferential \(\partial_C f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clarke stationarity does not imply local or global minimality and does not validate convex subgradient-inequality, averaging, or global objective-gap arguments.
